Zimbabwe—Prime Minister and Minister of State

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have much pleasure in informing the House that the Rt Hon
Morgan Tsvangirai MP, Prime Minister of the Republic of Zimbabwe, is within the
precincts of this Chamber. I am sure that members would wish that he be welcomed and
accorded a seat on the left of the Chair, a nd that the Hon Jameson Timba, Minister of
State, and the delegation in the Speaker’s gallery, also be welcomed.
The Rt Hon Morgan Tsvangirai, accompanied by the Minister for Primary Industries,
entered the Chamber and took a seat on the left of the Chair.
Statutory Holidays—Waitangi Day and Anzac Day
1. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement “My expectations are th at this will be a busy, hard three years’
work and we will need to deliver results for New Zealanders”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: On this side of the House, yes, and on the
other side of the House, I am sure that David Cunliffe is very busy. He sees it as 3 years
of hard work and is sure it will deliver a result.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will he and his caucus deliver results for hard-working New
Zealanders by supporting David Clark’s bill to have a day off on the Monday when
Waitangi Day and Anzac Day fall on a weekend?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with Tourism Industry Association chief executive
officer Martin Snedden, who said “Crea ting long weekends will boost New Zealand’s
economy in relevant years by stimulating domestic tourism.”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with Judith Collins that having a public holiday the
following Monday undermines Anzac Day and Waitangi Day commemorations?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think the Minister makes a very fair point.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he understand that hard-working New Zealanders think it is
fair to have a holiday on the Monday when the public holiday falls on a Sunday?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I understand the concerns New Z ealanders might have. I also
understand the issues at stake. There ar e many people who would feel very, very
strongly that Mondayisation w ould be taking away potentially from those very, very
significant days. Let us say this—[ Interruption] They are baying like a bunch of
banshees, but you had 9 years in Government and you did not do anything about it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Before I call Leader of the Opposition, I say that the Speaker
did not have the last 9 years in Government.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: In light of his last answer, coul d he answer how Christmas Day in
2010 was undermined by having a holiday the following week; and on that basis, would
he consider taking Monday away when Christmas Day falls on a weekend?
3884 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I can understand why David Shearer is focused on Christmas
Day, because that is the only day that Da vid Cunliffe takes off from plotting.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I think some attempt to address the question should be made.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I gave it my best shot. If one looks at the issue of
Mondayisation, yes, there will always be a ra nge of views. But I think there are many
New Zealanders who would say that when it comes to Waitangi Day and Anzac Day,
they are very significant, peculiar days to New Zealand, and therefore the honouring of
those days when they occur makes sense. I know the Labour Party members want to
take a holiday; it is pretty obvious from the amount of work they do not do. And good
news: you are in for a lot longer holiday than you are planning.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I hope the Speaker  is not in for a lot longer holiday than he
is planning. [Interruption] Enough said.
State-owned Assets, Sales—Government Policy
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement that “we don’t favour one group over another”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I stand by my full quote, which I made at
the National Party conference about the National Party, whic h was “We have tolerance
and respect for all New Zealanders a nd we don’t favour one group over another.”
Although it is not part of my ministerial responsibility, the point I was making is that we
are a broad church party and not aligned to a particular interest group such as unions.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is not paying the brokerage fees of retail investors in the asset
sales favouring the roughly 5 percent of Ne w Zealanders whom Treasury expects to
directly buy shares over the 95 percent of Ne w Zealanders who are not expected to buy
shares?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Government has a number of wide-ranging objectives in
terms of the mixed-ownership model programme . One of those is to  see as widespread
ownership as possible, by as many New Z ealanders as possible—for it to be as
accessible as possible. I need to check the point about whether we are paying brokerage
fees. I would be very surprised if we were doing that. We certainly have a loyalty bonus
aimed at those New Zealanders, if that is what the member means.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, is he aware that ther e is $56 million in the Budget
primarily to pay the brokerage fees to the selling syndicate; and why is it fair for all
taxpayers to cover the brokerage fees of the 5 percent?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would need to check that matter. I am sure the member is
probably incorrect in the assumption he is making. If he wants a detailed answer, he
would be better to put down a question to the Minister responsible.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why does the Government claim that asset sales are about mum
and dad investors, when Treasury’s numbers show that, in fact, 95 percent of mums and
dads would end up subsidising the 5 percent who can afford to buy shares?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I am not sure Treasury’s advice does show that. In fact,
I would reject that. I draw the attention of the member to the following, which is that of
the last 219 initial public offerings that we looked at, the Government of the day gave
retail incentives in 110 of them, and loyalty bonuses in 84. It is quite a widespread
technique used everywhere. This member seems, I have got to say, to be quite
incredible. Having spent the last year berating me for wanting to sell shares,
theoretically, to foreigners, which is not wh at I want to do, he is now berating me for
making sure I sell them to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why does the Government claim that asset sales would improve
electricity market competition, when the electricity provided by the publicly owned
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3885
power companies is already 12 percent cheaper than that from the private providers, and
privatisation would remove th at anchor on the market, and, hence, we would likely see
increased power prices?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Like many of the numbers that  the member quotes, those are
just rubbish. But if we go back to the broader issue, what re ally drives power prices is
the structure of the electric ity industry—something that this  Government has reformed.
That is why under the previous Labour G overnment power prices went up 72 percent
while those members sat on their hands, and under this Government they have gone up
14 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why does the Government claim that asset sales would improve
electricity market competition, when the re structuring that he just referred to was
possible only because the energy companies were State-owned enterprises, and once
they are made into mixed-ownership model companies the Government will lose the
capacity to perform exactly that kind of restructuring where it moves assets around?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Competition in a market is competition amongst all
participants. What the member has just said  is absolute rubbis h. He is saying that
competition exists because we happen currently, as a country, to 100 percent own
Meridian Energy, Mighty River Power, and Ge nesis, but he does not  count competition
that might be provided by Contact Energy, of which the Government has no ownership.
That is a ridiculous argument.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why does the Government clai m that asset sales are about
deepening New Zealand capital markets and getting Kiwis involved in the share market,
and then go and decide to list those companies on the Australian stock exchange; is it
because more Kiwis are leaving than ever before for Australia, under his
administration?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, a cynic might say it is in case the member moves back.
The Government has not made a decision yet about whether the companies will be
listed on the ASX. But, as I have said publicly  before, the advice is that that may be the
right thing to do, not because we will see a lot of trading on the ASX—eight of the top
10 New Zealand companies are listed on the New Zealand exchange and the ASX, and
the vast bulk of the trading in thos e companies takes place on the New Zealand
exchange—but because the mandate of some  Australian fund managers that buy shares
on behalf of New Zealanders as well as others requires them to be listed on the ASX. Of
course we can take that opportunity away, but , again, we would take away some of the
price competitiveness that others might enjoy if they bought those shares.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Given that the Government  has failed to convince New
Zealanders of the arguments around asset sa les, as shown by every major opinion poll,
is that because the Government actually does not ha ve very good reasons, and his
approach now is to say “Rubbi sh!” to anyone who disagrees with him, and to tell the
people of New Zealand: “We are simply goi ng to force it down your throat.” in a
Muldoonist way, just like previous National Governments have?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There are many analogies one could draw with me, but
Muldoon is probably not one of them. Let me  run the maths past the member. There
were a touch over a million New Zealanders who voted for the National Party at the
most recent general election, where front an d centre stage was th is policy, and last
weekend 79 protestors turned up to oppose it. And 1 million is greater than 79. If the
member cared enough about it, he would have g one out in the rain and protested, but he
was tucked up in his warm, insulated—t hanks to the National Government—house,
reading some leftie magazine he enjoys, in stead of being out there protesting with the
other 79.
3886 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012
Housing Affordability and Social Housing—Productivity Commission Report
3. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Finance : What reports has
he received on housing affordability?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Housing affordability is important for
fairness and for allocation of capital in the economy. The Produc tivity Commission
released a report on housing affordability that found that housing in New Zealand has
become increasingly unaffordable over the past decade. Real house prices almost
doubled between 2001 and 2007. In particular, it found that there is almost no building
of houses that are affordable for New Zealande rs in the lowest quartile of incomes. The
commission found that this affects communities and puts pressures on the
Government’s fiscal position, because the Gove rnment has very large subsidies to the
cost of housing.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What are some of the factors behind housing affordability issues in
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Productivity Commission found that the price of
housing has been driven up by a combin ation of rising demand and unresponsive
supply. Housing prices boomed in the 2000s, backed by large Government transfers,
strong population growth, and favourable terms of trade, but the supply of housing has
been unable to keep up with demand. We  agree with the Productivity Commission’s
view that urban planning has played a critical role in constraining the supply of land and
constraining the opportunity for higher-density development within cities.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Why does the Government regard the issue of housing affordability
as a priority?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: If we left the situation as we inherited it from the previous
Government, housing would be too expens ive for young, lower-income, and migrant
New Zealanders, who would find themselves  locked out of the housing market and
locked into poor and low-quality housing. This  Government made it the first inquiry of
the Productivity Commission when it was set up, and intends to follow through by
working with local government and with the planning and deve lopment industry to
improve housing affordability.
Denis O’Rourke: How confident is the Minister in the Social Housing Unit, when
the Productivity Commission report on afford able housing states: “Although the formal
objectives of the SHU are clear, its struct ure as a semi-autonomous body leaves room
for unclear priorities, mixed purposes and misaligned accountabilities.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We appreciate the advice of  the Productivity Commission.
The Social Housing Unit is a very early a ttempt to undo the substantial mess left in
social housing by the previous Labour Govern ment, with around about $5 billion worth
of houses in poor condition, the wrong size, and in the wrong place. They are not
enabling the taxpayer to help those New Z ealanders who are in serious housing need
and need assistance.
Denis O’Rourke: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was about how
confident the Minister was about those issues. I do not think he answered that question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That type of question asks for an  opinion, and the Minister gave his
opinion. He said that the views of the Produc tivity Commission were very valuable to
the Government. Therefore, obviously, it takes the views quite seriously. When asking
for an opinion like that, there is no particular answer to that kind of question.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Does he appreciate the advice of the chair of the Productivity
Commission, who said recently that the G overnment’s budget for social housing aimed
at making housing affordable for low-income New Zealanders is well short of the mark,
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3887
and does not meet current need, and that expa nding the role of soci al housing is at the
heart of addressing affordability?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I certainly do not agree with  the last remark, because,
actually, the heart of housing a ffordability is enabling all Ne w Zealanders, not just that
small minority who are in sign ificant housing need. But in re spect of the other remarks
that the commissioner has made, yes, we br oadly agree with them. I think even the
member has made some useful comments hersel f in the last few weeks to the effect that
if we want a proper allocation of capital in the economy, if we want to be more effective
in the way that we assist New Zealanders w ith housing, we need to rethink the current
models, and that is what we are doing.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What issues is the Government considering in preparing its
response to the Productivity Commission’s report on housing affordability?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government is looking at all the issues raised by the
Productivity Commission, which include land supply, resource and building consenting,
development contributions, liab ility rules, cost of buildi ng materials, and industry
structure. Actually, to that we would add the fiscal costs to the Government, which
include all of the housing subsidies, the implicit subsidy in the ownership of $15 billion
worth of Housing New Zealand Corporation assets, and the significant transfers through
Working for Families and other schemes, which are there partly to help New Zealand
households meet the excessive cost of housing.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: If the Minister does agree w ith the chair of the Productivity
Commission, why did he cut the budget for social housing over the next 3 years?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I would contest the Mini ster’s view about the social
housing budget being cut. Certainly—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: She’s not the Minister yet.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —the member’s views—she can put down a question to the
Minister of Housing about the detail. But in the interests of getting more assistance for
more New Zealanders more efficiently out  of the Housing New Zealand Corporation,
we are changing the way the money is use d, which means less focus on some of the
individual schemes the previous Government  had in place, and mo re focus on having
more larger providers of social housing.
Environment—Mackenzie Sustainable Futures Trust
4. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
When his office had a “quick look at the matters involved” with regard to the funding of
the Mackenzie Sustainable Futures Trust, wh om did they speak to and what documents
did they look at to arrive at their conclu sion that “we did not fi nd anything that raised
concerns to us”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Between my office and the Minister for the
Environment’s office a review was undertaken of the documents released to the member
under the Official Information Act, the funding arrangements, and the scope of the work
undertaken. From that review, we were satisf ied that the matter did not warrant further
investigation.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why did he and his office not c onsider that the email from Guy
Salmon on 6 September 2011 was a cause for c oncern, given that in that email Mr
Salmon sought to pre-empt the outcome of th e independent panel’s consideration of the
trust’s application to the Community Envir onment Fund, an email that led a ministry
official to say that the trust was “pressuring the ministry”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We would reject the assertions  that the member has made. I
make two points. Firstly, the Community Environment Fund funding was actually never
used. I am advised that around 15 months pa ssed between the trus t initially seeking
3888 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012
Community Environment Fund funding and th e final decision being made not to
provide it. That might be rushed, in the Labour Party’s time and thinking, but 15 months
is not rushed under this Government.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why did he and his office not c onsider the statement from Guy
Salmon in the email of 6 September 2011 to be  a concern, when that statement reads:
“Nick gave me to understand that  he was going to establish collaborative processes as a
specific priority to be funded in the forthcoming … round; however there was no sign of
that on the application form. I worry that Nick  is so overloaded that  he has not actually
been on top of looking after this project.”, and does that not sound like the trust believes
that it was being considered differently from other projects?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. It sounds like a couple of things: firstly, concern that Nick
Smith had an awful lot on his plate, which he did because he was a very busy Minister
at the time; and, secondly, a ge nuine view from the Minister  that he thought the right
way to go was a collaborative approach—tha t that would be appropriate for that
mechanism to be set up—and that possibl y Community Environment Fund funding was
the right way to actua lly fund that. I simply make th is point: maybe Grant Robertson
would like to go and ask Charles Chauvel what Charles Chauvel said—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. Order!

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why did his office not consider that there may be issues of
concern about the treatment of a trust chaired by a National Party MP, when a Ministry
for the Environment official said in an  email dated Monday, 29 August 2011 that the
registering of the trust on the society’s register was managed in quick time as a result of
“a special favour request”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There is nothing unusual about tr ying to establish a process to
resolve an important issue. This issue was an issue of great concern. It had over 10,000
submissions. I simply say to the member: go and ask Charles Chauvel and see what he
said at the Environmental Defence Society conference.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he accept that the f unding of important and useful
collaborative processes for dealing with environmental issues still needs to be subject to
the proper processes and transparency?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and that is why the Community Environment Fund in the
end was not used to fund the project, as the member should know. I simply say to the
member go and ask Charles Chauvel what he said at the Environmental Defence Society
conference.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he believe on the basis of th e investigation of his office that
the Mackenzie Sustainable Futures Trust received the same treatment as other
applicants for ministry funding, particularly in light of the Ministry for the Environment
indicating in official documents that it had spent 200 hours of staff time on the trust
application between March and October 2011?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The trust did not get funding from the Community
Environment Fund. The trust ultimately got  funding at the disc retion of the Chief
Executive of the Ministry for the Envir onment. There is no question that the
Government believed that th e collaborative approach was th e right way to  go. It was
estimated to be a tenth of the cost of going through a litigious process. It is also true that
the ministry thought that a better way to go was through the court, and the Government
thought that spending $2.6 million to resolve something that could be approved through
a collaborative process was the better way to go. And I simply say to the member go
and ask Charles Chauvel what he said.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why does the Prime Minister think that Ministry for the
Environment officials raised serious concerns about the funding of the project?
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3889

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There were people within the ministry who did not like the
collaborative approach and wanted to go to c ourt—they wanted to go to court. They are
welcome to their view, but we do not listen to every official’s view. And not so long
ago I remember being in this House and he aring Helen Clark say she did not get any
ideas from officials; she got them from the Guardian. I say to the member go and ask
Charles Chauvel what he said at the Environmental Defence Society conference.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek leave of the House to table three documents. The first of
those is an email from a Ministry for the Environment offici al, dated Monday, 29
August 2011, that says that the societies register applicatio n of the trust was processed
as a result of a special favour request.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek leave of the House to table an email from Guy Salmon,
dated Tuesday, 6 September 2011, to Jacqui Dean, in which he seeks to pre-empt the
outcome of the community environment fund process.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I seek leave of the House to table a time line developed by the
Ministry for the Environment on funding of the trust, which includes the statement that
the funds management team alone estimates  that between March and October 2011 it
spent an estimated 200 hours working on funding of the trust.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Child Abuse and Neglect—Government Measures to Address
5. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
initiatives has the Government put in place to better protect children?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Protecting children
from abuse and neglect is and has been a ma jor priority for this Government. We have
introduced a number of significant initiatives that are making a real difference. Just in
the last few months, for example, we have a nnounced the first roll-out of extra social
workers in schools, and 96 more Child, Yout h and Family social workers on the front
line. The “failure to protect” amendment to the Crimes Act has come into effect, and the
Privacy (Information Sharing) Bill is progressing through the House.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How is the Government suppor ting professionals working with
children to recognise and respond to signs of child abuse and neglect?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As part of our initiatives to better protect children, we
funded NGO Child Matters to run 1-day workshops around New Zealand, providing
training to health, education, a nd social service pr ofessionals to iden tify signs of child
abuse. To date it has delivered over 96 workshops reaching over 2,700 professionals.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can she confirm that her answers to written questions are correct,
and that the number of child  protection cases that Child, Youth and Family has deemed
serious enough to prompt further action has increased over th e past 4 years by 42
percent to almost 58,000 cases, yet the number of social workers in reality has increased
only by 50?
3890 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: As I said, we recently made announcements of those 50,
and we have got 96 who will be there overall. Yes, notifications have increased. Also,
though, if you like, the false positives—so the number of notifications we get—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: That’s further action required.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I am just saying also those ones that we do not have to
follow up. Over the last 8 years, from memory —I do not have the number in front of
me—notifications have actually increased by about 400 percent overall.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: What reports has she received that  support the Government’s focus on
protecting children?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I welcome the coroner’s recommendations, which
validate the initiatives we have already in troduced and the work we are currently doing
as part of the white paper on vulnerable ch ildren. None of the recommendations come
as a surprise, as they have been raised in  previous inquiries and in submissions on the
green paper. A response will be coming forthwith.
Government Financial Position—Effect on Transport Projects
6. ANDREW WILLIAMS (NZ First)  to the Minister of Finance : Does the
Government still intend to achieve a budget surplus by 2014/15; if so, how?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes; we want to achieve this by
keeping firm control on the Government’s costs, which we believe is the situation at the
moment. Budget forecasts show that the tax revenue, which is inclined to be more
volatile, is on track for surplus in 2014-15.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Are cutbacks to major Governme nt roading programmes such as
the Ōtaki to Levin expressway—which wa s scrapped in favour of upgrading the
existing highway, with the sudden saving of $300 million—now the only hope the
Government has of getting anywhere near th e target of a Budget surplus in 2014-15; if
not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Can the Minister confirm th at scrapping the four-lane
expressway from Ōtaki to Levin will not be the first of a series of cu tbacks to roading
programmes in order to achieve a Budget surplus in the 2014-15 year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, if the member wants to debate the details of what
decisions have actually been made about the Ōtaki to Levin highway, then he could
direct those questions more properly to the Mi nister of Transport. But what I have put
out to the Minister is that decisions about roading are ma de on their own merits. They
are not made in the context of the need fo r the Government to find money for the 2014-
15 surplus.

Oil and Gas Extraction—Hydraulic Fracturing in Taranaki
7. GARETH HUGHES (Green)  to the Minister of Energy and Resources : Does
he stand by his statement on the Campbell Live 9 February programme on fracking that,
“In Taranaki, it’s actually b een done very, very well. Ther e’s been no effect on the
environment whatsoever”?
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3891

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: In context, yes;
obviously, everything has an environmental ef fect. I am interested in environmental
effects that are significant. As I understand it, the Taranaki Regi onal Council stands by
its position. There have been no significan t environmental effects caused by hydraulic
fracturing in Taranaki.

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: Is groundwater contamination at four Kapuni fracking sites, which
has left water there unfit for potable water or stock use, an example of fracking that has
been done very, very well?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Well, the statement is incorrect. In the past, some pits were
used to receive fluids from fracked wells. Ho wever, I am advised that the fluid returns
were highly unlikely to be the source. The monitoring undertaken shows this is a legacy
issue. It happened in the past. It is highl y unlikely to be asso ciated with hydraulic

items.text: Is the common use of flare pits in  Taranaki an example of fracking

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I
tērā wiki i kōrero au ki te Whare kia aro nui ki te āhuatanga o Te Wiki o Te Reo M āori.
Kua rongo ake a “O-tacky”, kua rongo ake a “Tarra-nacky”. Ko t āku īnoi kia tika r ā nō
te whakahua o ng ā īngoa Māori i t ēnei wiki m ō Te Reo M āori. Ko te ingoa e tika ana,
ko Ōtaki, i tēnei wā ko Taranaki. Kia ora tātau.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker. Last week I said to the House that it should pay
attention to the situation that relates to M āori Language Week. I have just heard “O-
tacky” and “Tarra-nacky”. My plea  is that the pronunciation of M āori names must be
correct in this week for the M āori language. The proper name is Ōtaki and at this point
in time it is Taranaki. Greetings to us.]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the goodwill in the member’s point of order. It is not
strictly a point of order, but under the circumstances I think his point is well made.
Where did we get to? The honourable Minist er is to answer. Does the Minister
remember the question asked?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I am happy to answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Phil Heatley.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: A number of groups have views on this practice and,
indeed, on oil and gas exploration. Unfortunately, on the far right they want to bring out
the bulldozers. We, as a party, are saying no. We want to be environmentally sensible

Fortunately, we in the National Party—and the Labour Party, which promoted deep-sea

items.speaker: Gareth Hughes
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. It was a clear question. It was

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Child Health—Improved Services
8. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister of Health : What progress has been
made in providing improved child health services?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The Government has made strong
progress in improving health services for children. Immunisation is  now at a record
level of 93 percent for 2-year-olds. There are free doctors’ visits for children under 6,
day and night, 7 days a week, and a $24 milli on programme to address rheumatic fever,
and we have rescued the B4 School checks programme, which has seen almost 140,000
children being given free health and development checks before they start school. The
Government’s policies are not so much about  closing the gaps as  lifting for all,
especially those most in need, and this is well demonstrated by the immunisation
success story. While the immunisation rate for our children has lifted, the increase in the
immunisation rate for Māori has lifted much greater, from 73 percent to 92 percent, and
for children of Pacific Island ethnicity, from  80 percent to an unprecedented 97 percent.
In terms of income—this is very interest ing—the poorest income groups have exactly
the same immunisation rate as the wealthiest groups: 94 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: What progress has been made w ith the new programme to reduce
rheumatic fever, a Third World dis ease particularly prevalent in M āori and Pacific
Island communities?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think the first point I need to  make is that rheumatic fever
can develop into a life-threatening heart di sease and have the patient on 10 years of
monthly penicillin injections. But this ve ry serious Third World disease can be
prevented, and it is one of th e National-led Government’s key result areas to reduce the
incidence of rheumatic fever by two-thirds  by 2017. What I can announce today is that
the largest initiative ever in South Auck land to deal with rheumatic fever will be
launched on Friday. It is going to be opening at the Rongomai School in Ōtara, which
will be the first of 18 school-based clinic s in South Auckland. Clinics will open in
Manurewa, M āngere, and Papakura schools. The clin ics will check throats and skin
infections, provide antibiotics, and provide  access to services for healthy housing and
injury prevention—a great achievement for New Zealand.

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: What action is he taking to ensure that all rural areas, including
Invercargill and Lumsden, have access to free after-hours urgent health-care for children
under 6?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As the member will know, the scheme is not compulsory, and
the district health boards are negotiating that with various localities. We are currently at
just over 90 percent of the country providing that access. That is a tremendous
achievement for free after-hours health-care for under-sixes, and I look to progress in
the southern region with those particular communities in the next while.
New Zealand - Australia Migration—18 to 30 Age Range
9. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement regarding migration to Austra lia “What’s the point of standing in the
airport crying about it?”; if so, how many of the 158,167 people that have migrated to
3894 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012
Australia since November 2008, as reported by Statistics NZ, are from 18 to 30 years of
age in number and percentage terms?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Since November 2008, 61,937 people
aged 18 to 30—about 39 percent of the total. Yes, I do stand by my statement, because I
think it is important New Zealand gets  on with expanding industries, supporting
businesses, and creating jobs, so that t hose young people feel like they have more
choices in a country going ahead, not one that  is spending and borrowing more than it
can afford.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can New Zealand prosper when so many of our youngest
and brightest are choosing to work in Australi a rather than contribute to New Zealand’s
economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: New Zealand can prosper if, for instance, the Opposition
supports the Government’s push to expand our oil and gas and minerals industries—
exactly the industries that those young New Zealanders are going to work in in
Australia. So if it is good enough for them to  stay here, it is good enough for us to have
those kinds of jobs for them.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: When will he acknowledge that too many young New
Zealanders are leaving because under his Government they lack hope and opportunity in
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not accept that. The fact is in recent years the Australian
economy has had higher growth rates than  New Zealand’s. The migration flows
between the two countries have generally corr elated with those growth rates. The New
Zealand Government is pushing to accelerate our growth rate in part by expanding the
kind of industry that has been at the core of Australia’s success, and that is its resource-
based industries, where those young New Zeal anders are going to get those jobs. Why
can we not have them in those jobs here?

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Does he agree that the Cant erbury rebuild offers opportunities
for young Kiwis to stay and work in New Z ealand; if so, how does the Government’s
record of spending a paltry $8 million on post- earthquake skills training in Canterbury,
out of a total of $42 million allocated, help young Kiwis get the ski lls needed to fill
those jobs and stay in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think there are two parts to that answer. In the first place,
the Government looks to be heading to spend somewhere around $13 billion to $14
billion in Christchurch, and that will prov ide lots of jobs for young New Zealanders.
Secondly, in respect of training places, there are more training places available than
there are young New Zealanders willing and ab le to take them up, and we expect to
maintain that situation for some time yet.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that National campaigned so vociferously on reducing the
brain drain to Australia, w hy do his targets by which he can be held to account not
include any target or milestone for clos ing the wage gap with Australia, nor for
decreasing the number of New Zealanders moving from New Zealand to Australia?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The number of New Zealanders  going to Australia can be
measured every day. The one way to stem th at flow is to support businesses that make
the decisions to invest more and employ another person. That is why so many New
Zealanders did not vote for th e Labour Party in the last  election—because they know
that it does not take that approach.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is he proud that the Statistics New Zealand figures show that
National’s policies are turning Generation Y into “Generation Oz”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is not what the figures show. I am very proud that
National’s policies are turning round and re pairing the damage done by the last
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3895
Government to this economy, and are building a brighter future for thousands of young
New Zealanders.
Business Research and Development—Advanced Technology Institute
10. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister of Science and

items.speaker: Innovation
items.text: How will the Advanced Technology In stitute boost business-led research
and development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Advanced
Technology Institute is designed to be a one-stop shop for businesses’ research and
development needs. It will support firms at di fferent stages of development, from start-
ups to established research and developmen t performers, to innova te in response to
domestic and international market opportunities. The Advanced Technology Institute
will consolidate services that were previously only available across a number of entities,
if at all. These include services such as  product testing analysis and certification,
research and development work, access to business research and development funding,
commercialisation assistance, and intell ectual property advi ce. The Advanced
Technology Institute will also broker connec tions for businesses with the specialised
expertise, equipment, and faci lities they need to develop new or better products or
services, whether located within New Zealand or further afield.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How does the establishment of the Advanced Technology Institute and
the Government’s commitment to science and innovation compare with the previous
Government’s spending on research and development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Actually we have made tr emendous progress given tight
financial conditions. Total Government sp ending on research and innovation funding
has increased dramatically since 2007-08. In  fact, funding has increased 46 percent in
that period, from $848 million to $1,241 million in 2012-13. We have also managed to
increase the share of business-led research  and development expenditure from just 8
percent of the total in 2009-10 to an estimated nearly  20 percent in 2012-13. Combined
with these funding increases, the creation of the Advanced Technology Institute will
help better link business a nd science and help create new, high-tech  products and
services, which are crucial to help New Zealand grow faster.
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Minister—Use of Powers
11. Hon LIANNE DALZIEL (Labour—Christchurch East)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
items.text: Why did he use section 27 of the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Act 2011  to amend the Canterbury Regional Policy Statement
instead of using the Order in Council provision s of the Act or developing the recovery
strategy or a recovery plan?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
inserted chapter 12A into the regional policy statement to ensure that there was enough
easily consentable land for new subdivisions in the Greater Christchurch area. I did so
with the encouragement of, a nd in consultation with, local authorities. Section 27 was
seen as the quickest way to ensure delivery of new residential sec tions on safe ground
for the many people in Christchurch affected  by New Zealand’s largest natural disaster.
I am passionate about effecting as fast as possible a recovery for people in the Greater
Christchurch area. I note that the judge said that he belie ved I had acted in good faith. I
am pleased that the decision has left in place the new subdivisions that were fast-tracked
by my decision. I will now consider fully what the judge’s deci sion means and what
implications it has.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Does he stand by his statem ent that the powers under the
legislation are “essentially reserve powers a nd there will be checks and balances on the
3896 Questions for Oral Answer 25 Jul 2012
use of these powers so the public can have confidence they are be ing used wisely and
with restraint.”, and why did the court not think that he wa s using them wisely and with
restraint when he acted outside the powers of the legislation?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: That is the current judgment and I accept that.
However, there is going to be  some consideration of exactly what that judgment means.
What I would say is that there was a need  for new subdivisions to be enacted in
Canterbury quickly. Even the member herself was calling for that at a number of points,
as were some of her colleagues. The urban development strategy, on which the change
was based, was created through a very long consultation pro cess that dated back to
2004. During that time there were numerous  community consultations undertaken by
the strategy partners and there were so me 3,250 submissions on growth management
options for the Greater Christchurch area. Th at resulted in plan change 1, which was
promulgated in 2007. There were around some  700 submissions lodged in response to
that, and there were hearings held thr oughout 2009. The matter was then taken to the
Environment Court, and that is where it was stuck at the time of the earthquakes in 2010
and 2011. I worked after that very closely with the elected representatives to try to come
up with a solution that did not mean th at we were cherry-picking, through the
Government legislation, exactly which subdi visions went where. We chose a solution
that the community itself had chosen. The judge has said that we used the wrong
provision. I cannot challenge th at and I wish to say no furt her about that, but I would
note that there are thousands of sections available now that w ould not have been
available under any other process.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Does the Minister agree that  the court upheld the judicial
review because the Minister had chosen an  option that had none of the checks and
balances that he had told the people of New Zealand would be in place?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think my answer to the previous question absolutely
rejects that proposition. The fact is that  I did not accept the lobbying of individual
property owners. I did not accept the offers of individual property owners. Instead I
accepted—

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not interject or take a
point of order during th e very lengthy answer that we had before. The specific question
that I asked was whether the reason for the c ourt’s decision was the lack of checks and
balances that he had said would be in place.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept the goodwill in the member’s point of order, but in the
Minister’s answer I think he is being very careful not to comment on the legal
implications of a judicial decision. It is not  for a Minister to s econd-guess why a judge
may have made a decision the judge has made. I think the Minister is trying to be very
careful not to comment on the judge’s decision, not to offe r reasons why the judge may
or may not have made the decision made. That  is why I allowed the Minister somewhat
more latitude, and I am sure the experienced  member would know th at the Minister has
to be very careful in that regard. I see it be ing quite difficult for the Minister to try to
answer too precisely what the member has asked. Has the Hon Gerry Brownlee finished
the answer?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, I think so.

items.speaker: Hon Lianne Dalziel
items.text: Does the Minister recall identifying the checks and balances
that he said would be in place and from which the public could take comfort: the four-
person independent review panel, the cro ss-party forum, the forum of community
leaders, appeal rights, and the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority being subject
to the Official Information Act? And can he confirm that, in fact, none of those
particular checks and balances were in play when he made his decision?
25 Jul 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3897

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: If one was to dissect the Act and the various reasons
for the powers, then all of those things w ould be true. But section 27 stands on its own
and we believed that it was quite appropriate to move thi ngs in a rapid way. One of the
extraordinary things I will point to in th e judgment—and I make no comment on it—is
that the judge has said that he felt that th e decision was about matters that had existed
prior to the earthquake event and would endure beyond the eart hquake event, and
therefore the recovery powers were inappropriate. Matters that were in place prior to the
earthquake event were the faults undernea th Christchurch, a nd, secondly, we would
hope that all the decision made by the Cant erbury Earthquake Recovery Authority, in
conjunction with local authorities, Ng āi Tahu, and other individual partners, do endure
beyond this earthquake event. The judge has ruled that we used the wrong provisions
under the Act.
Biosecurity Management—Government Initiatives
12. SHANE ARDERN (National—Taranaki - King Country)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Primary Industries
items.text: What recent announcements has he made to further improve New
Zealand’s biosecurity system?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: On Friday I announced
that 11 new biosecurity detector dogs would join the front line this year. This is a 42
percent increase in the number of detector dogs active at our border. Detector dogs and
their handlers are another im portant part of our biosecur ity system’s front line. The

and plants that X-rays may miss.

items.speaker: Shane Ardern
items.text: What additional improvements is  the Minister making to New

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I strongly believe that New Zealand’s biosecurity system is
the best in the world, and that the Ministry  for Primary Industries does an outstanding
job. Having said that, neither I nor the Minist ry for Primary Industries are content with
simply maintaining this world-leading sy stem. We are continua lly looking to make
improvements, and they include such thi ngs as adding 40 additional jobs to the
biosecurity front line in Auckland a nd Wellington next month, progressing the
Biosecurity Law Reform Bill through the House, and progressing a number of
Government-industry agreements. That is why biosecurity expenditure in the last year
was the highest that it has been in the last decade, and almost double what it was in

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Does he agree with the findings  of the Sapere Research Group
report into the outbreak of Psa in New Zeal and that the lack of consistency in the
Ministry of Agriculture and Fo restry staff’s individualised approaches led to “reactive
and fragmented assessment of the risks of Ps a across individual pathways”; if so, what
action will he take to ensure there is gr eater cohesion between Ministry for Primary

Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, Minister—Judicial Decision Regarding Use of
Powers

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from the Hon Lianne Dalziel seeking to
debate under Standing Order 386 the High Court ruling that the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery stepped outside th e legal limits of his powers under the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act 2011 in making his decision to amend the 1998
Canterbury Regional Policy Statement. The mann er in which the Minister exercises his
powers under the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Act is undoubtedly an important
issue for the House because of the considerable nature of the powers the Act grants.
However, for there to be an urgent debate there must be a particular case of recent
occurrence involving the administrative or ministerial responsibility of the Government.
The Minister’s decisions were yesterday set aside by the High Court, and an application
for a judicial review granted. There is no mini sterial responsibility for a decision of the
High Court. The urgent debate procedure is a way of holding the Government to
account for matters of recent occurrence. Th ere can be no particular case of recent
occurrence in the absence of any furthe r decision by the Minister, which, in all
probability, may not be forthcoming until the outcome of the judicial review is known.
The application is therefore declined.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: I raise a point of order,
Mr Speaker. I am actually seeking your assist ance on this, because I am a little unclear.
There have been instances where snap debates have been given in the House as a result
of a decision of a court. In this particular case, it is a judicial re view of a Minister’s
decision. The Minister made th e decision last y ear and would not be making another
decision in response to the court’s decision, because the court’s decision did not allow
aspects of it to be overturned. So certain aspects of it, as I set out in my letter, have been
allowed to continue, and they  are the developments that are taking place in, I think,
three of the particular subdivisi ons. So there is no need for the Minister to take another
step.
The problem is that there was a lot of  public controversy surrounding the very
extensive powers in the legislation, and I think this Parliament does have a duty to
oversee how the legislation is actually operati ng in practice. I think the Speaker will
recall that there was considerable debate, ce rtainly on this side of  the House, as to
whether we would agree to the legislation going through, which we did, but we feel that
the scrutiny is required. So that is why I have put forward the letter.
25 Jul 2012 Urgent Debates Declined 3899

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not want to risk the contribution to a debate by a point of order.
But the member herself has pointed out that the court has made a certain decision to set
aside something, and there is no ministerial de cision at the moment. If the Minister had
made an immediate decision in response to that, then there would have been, indeed,
perhaps a matter for the House to debate ur gently. But the court has made a decision
simply to set aside a decision of the Minister . The Minister, or the Minister on behalf of
the Government, has made no response whatsoev er to that, and therefore there is no
matter of recent occurrence for this House to have an urgent debate on. That is why the
Speaker’s decision is made the way it is.
The member may well be right that there may well be interest in the ongoing powers
that the particular Act confe rred on the Minister, but that is a matter for debate under
normal opportunities when the House has a chance to debate matters. It is not something
that requires the House to set aside its busin ess today. And that is the test. The member
is asking that the House set aside its business to day so that this particular debate can be
held. That is a high test that is required, and it sometimes is met, indeed, by the urgency
of a matter where there is ministerial res ponsibility. But in this case there is no
particular urgency, because the Government  has not actually made any decision that
complies with the requirement for it to be a case of recent occurrence.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business. Kiwis have got a good idea of what a fair go means—an
attachment to the idea that no matter wh ere you come from, no matter what your
background, you will get the chance and the opp ortunity to get ahead and achieve your
potential. But with this Government it is clearly not what you know; it is who you
know. If we look at the front bench of the Natio nal Government it is definitely not what
they know—we can see that from over here —but it is who they know. This is a
Government governing in the interests of the few—the wealthy few.
Let us just take asset sales as one example.  It is a huge transfer  of wealth from the
vast bulk of the population of New Zeala nd to those who can a fford to pay—to those
who have got the $1,000. It is  a transfer from the panel beater in Waitakere—
“Waitakere man”, if you like, or “Waitake re woman”—who has a stake in those assets
today. That is being taken away by this Na tional Government and handed to the share
traders of Parnell. But, more than that, th e loyalty scheme that is now in place means
that the panel beater pays tw ice, because they are funding the costs of transferring the
shares to the New Zealanders who can afford them. This process will widen the gap
between the rich and the poor, which is something that this Government has no
compunction about doing.
We all know that the beneficiaries of the asset sale programme are the banks and the
consultants who are raking in millions of dolla rs to sell off what New Zealanders have
built up over generations. They are the same consultants and contractors who are
milking the public sector purse for all it is worth, because this Government thinks that
the best way to say whether the public sector is working is to work out what the
headcount is. Well, the Government depart ments are responding. They are reducing the
headcount all right, and the money is going stra ight to consultants and contractors. It is
spiralling out of control.
The National Government seems to have got its messages confused. When New
Zealanders say they like the idea of looking out for their mates, they do not mean the
National Government lining the pockets of its  friends at the expe nse of hard-working
men and women across New Zealand. Then, in  a zero Budget, somehow or other the
Government finds $40 million for private tr aining establishments. Funding cuts in
3900 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
education, bigger class sizes, no allowances for postgraduate students, but $40 million
for private education.
National says it wants to crack down on welfare. Well,  how about starting with a
crackdown on corporate welfare? This Governme nt is governing in the interests of the
few, and not the many. The stench of cronyism  that pervades this Government is as
strong as the smell of the brakes on Hekia Parata’s tyres as she reversed on class sizes.
Conflict of interest and cronyism is a l ong roll-call in this Government. Stephen
McElrea, the Prime Minister’s electorate chair, who is on the board of New Zealand On
Air, was interfering in decisions about prog ramming straight befo re an election. There
was a loan to MediaWorks from Steven Joyce, the man who knows a lot about that
company—$43 million in that company just happ ens to allow DJ Key to spin his discs
just before the election. Then we have got  the appointment of Katherine Rich to the
Health Promotion Agency. Katherine Rich  is a highly capable person, but she has
another job. She runs the Food and Grocery Council.
But it is more than that. There are two other members of the Health Promotion
Agency, Lee Mathias and Jamie Simpson, who ar e, respectively, the electorate chairs of
Sam Lotu-Iiga and Gerry Brownlee. You may well ask what qualification Gerry
Brownlee’s electorate chair has to be on th e Health Promotion Agency. Well, I can tell
you what it is. He is an insurance broker. That  is the qualification that he has got. It is
jobs for the boys. We can go on. There is the ACC and Bronwyn Pullar saga, and the
Skycity and pokies for legislation deal. This Government is full of cronyistic deals and
conflicts of interest.
A key player in the ACC saga was Nick Smith, who now finds hi mself right in the
middle of the latest bout of cronyism and conflicts of interest—the funding of the
Mackenzie Sustainable Futures Trust. Let me say for the record that I want to
acknowledge the great work of the many comm unity groups that have been involved in
the collaborative process down there. My concerns are not about them. My concerns are
about a trust, launched at  the National Party Bluegreen s conference, chaired by a
National MP, and directly funded by a Nationa l Minister, and about what that funding
says about the transparency and accountability of this Government.
The Prime Minister wants to sweep this unde r the carpet. For him, the ends justify
the means, no matter what. But our reputation as a country with a transparent Public
Service must be jealously guarded.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.role: Minist er for Arts, Culture and Heritage

items.text: I found the allegations of cronyism a bit rich, especially at times where I seem to be a
one-person employment agency for former  Labour MPs. But I want to start by
acknowledging and paying tribute to Margaret Mahy, one of our great literary figures,
who died on Monday. Her books were translated  into a dozen languages, and I am very
pleased to see that Joy Cowley and other writers are planning an hour-long tribute to her
at the Frankfurt Book Fair in October, where New Zealand will be the country of
honour.
Last weekend I went to the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra in Wellington, which
performed Wagner’s Valkyrie in honour of another grea t New Zealander, Lloyd
Morrison. Nothing more exposes the inaccura cy of headlines that the New Zealand
Symphony Orchestra could be axed than the fact that I sat through 5½ hours of Wagner
on a Sunday afternoon. Every New Zealande r should support and be proud of this
institution, although, as Michael Cullen said to me yesterday, there will always be some
people—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Sir Michael.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: —Sir Michael; I apologise—who say that
orchestras are a waste of money and that th ere are some who say that the second violins
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3901
should be abolished because they are an unn ecessary duplication of services. I was very
impressed by the singers at the concert, although the tenor could learn a thing or two
from a certain member of this House, who I am not allowed to bring into the debate but
whose musical virtuosity is known to and appreciated by us all, and I am not referring to
Brendan Horan.
Last weekend we had a very successful  National Party conference in Auckland.
Spirits were high, and the protests were s cant. Nothing makes left-wing protesters
abandon their cause faster than light drizzle. The mood of the public was positive, and it
is because this Government is getting th ings done for New Z ealand. We are settling
historical grievances with iwi, we ar e rebuilding Christchurch, we are improving
infrastructure, we are paying down debt, and we are strengthe ning New Zealand’s
capital markets. This will be a very busy 3 years for this Government, and we will
deliver results for New Zealanders.
The Labour Party members have been very busy, as well, staring at their own navels.
They have just finished a momentous review , not of how to grow the economy or make
the tax system work better but of how much  of a voting share Helen Kelly should have
in picking potential Prime Ministers. I thin k they have settled on 20 percent. David
Shearer has put in place a new organisational structure to cement his future as leader.
Rather than plotting in the shadows and brie fing TV3, Labour’s roll -call of leadership
challengers will now have to write to the party’s governing board to initiate a spill, with
the support of two-thirds of the caucus. Forward-thinking members like David Cunliffe
will protest that his campaign website is a more 21 st century way of signalling his
intentions than old-fashioned letter wr iting, and Grant R obertson, that great
internationalist currently temporarily reside nt in Wellington Cent ral, probably thinks
that a text from New York will suffice.
Mr Shearer is a traditionalist. He has c onsolidated his position. He stands on the
brink of greatness, at the threshold of ensu ring his tenure as the longest-serving Leader
of the Opposition in Labour Party history. Mr  Robertson will also reach another great
milestone—perhaps not the one he was after— and will be remembered as the longest-
serving deputy leader. Mr Shearer may justif y the odds to be known as one of the great
tacticians of New Zealand politics. He ha s quietly outmanoeuvred  Mr Robertson, who
has stacked the party’s headquarters and parliamentary offices with his loyalists. But Mr
Shearer has changed the rules of the game. I do not mean to say that Mr Robertson will
never make it to the top job; in fact, he has often struck me as—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: He’s obsessed with me.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I am not obsessed with him. He has often
struck me as the Gordon Brown of New Zealand’s social democracy. And I am not
suggesting that Mr Shearer and Mr Robertson are not close. A number of media profiles
that accompanied their ascent to the Labour l eadership noted their similarities. They are
very much the Noel and Liam Gallagher of the Labour Party. But there is no oasis for
the Labour Party; it is all desert.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What band are they from, Minister?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: Oasis. As I said, there is no oasis for the
Labour Party; it is all desert. It has been a week of triumph for Mr Shearer, out of the
limelight, away from the glare of public attention, which he does leave to Mr Robertson.
He has sorted out his legacy.
But how irrelevant it all seems when one compares that with the achievements of our
great Prime Minister and his Governmen t: on the one hand an inward-looking party,
focusing on how to deal with party challe ngers, and on the other hand a party and a
Government that are interested only in a brighter future for New Zealand.
3902 General Debate 25 Jul 2012

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: E te M āngai o te Whare, t ēnā koe.
Over the weekend Government Minister afte r Government Minister  was rolled out at
the National Party conference to attack th e Greens. Either National members have
nothing to say about their own economic achieve ment or they must be pretty scared of
the support the Greens are getting, to have spent so much time at their conference
attacking us—or maybe both are true. Although  National likes to talk up its economic
management, it has actually bungled its way through the past 4 years. Under its watch,
debt has skyrocketed, and many New Zealande rs have lost their jobs. National came
into office with zero net Government debt, and it is now $40 billion—that is right,
billion—in the hole. That is the biggest borrowing binge in New Zealand’s history.
We hear a lot of excuses from National a bout the difficult financial times, but what
exactly has been National’s brilliant economic response? It decided to borrow $2 billion
to give tax cuts to the rich, it is borrowi ng another $1.5 billion to subsidise polluters,
and it is splurging $12 billion on economically  irrational motorways. National oversaw
63,000 more Kiwis lose their jobs. Unempl oyment is increasing under National.
National believes that GDP growth is the be -all and end-all, but it continually misses its
Budget growth targets. Let us  be clear about this: John Key has overseen the worst
economic growth record in at least half a century.
What National is scared of is that the Gr een Party offers a serious alternative. Our
smart Green economics plan is jobs rich, i nnovative, environmentally sustainable, New
Zealand - owned, and long term. The UK’s biggest business lobby group, the
Confederation of British Industry, has just re leased a report showing the billions of
dollars that green growth can add to the economy. The director-general, John Cridland,
said: “with the right policies in place, green business will be a major pillar of our future
growth.” National certainly is not going for growth; its dirty, grey plan is jobs poor,
derivative, environmentally destructive, foreign-owned, and short term.
John Key and Steven Joyce, who have  ineptly stood by as 63,000 Kiwis have
become unemployed, like to lecture us about the need for job-creating policies, but the
truth—the fact—is that their policies have  led to more unemployment, whereas our
policies create more jobs than theirs. Investing in public transport is jobs rich. For every
dollar invested in public transport, it creates twice as many jobs as every dollar spent on
motorways. National is wasting $12 billion on uneconomic motorways that increase our
dependency on imported oil and create very few jobs. The Greens will invest in a
sustainable, smart transport system that gets us off our oil addiction and creates twice as
many jobs as investing in motorways.
Sustainable, clean energy creates three times as many jobs—dollar for dollar—than
investing in fossil fuels, which is this G overnment’s obsession. Not only is investing in
sustainable energy the right thing to do for the climate and our future but it creates more
jobs now. Twenty-thousand manufacturing jobs have disappeared under National, as the
Reserve Bank’s myopic focus on inflation dooms us to a current account deficit. The
Greens will grow the manufactur ing sector by reforming monetary policy so that our
manufacturers have a level playing field at home and overseas.
Bereft of ideas, National is selling assets  to try to patch up its botched economic
management. Its plan B is to deface our na tional parks and drill our oceans for fossil
fuels. Mining employs just 5,500 people—that is it. You would have to increase the
amount of mining fivefold just to replace the jobs that have been lost in manufacturing
while this National Party has been in Government.
Tourism and agriculture employ 92,000 a nd 97,000 people, respectively. These
industries depend on our “clean, green” brand and bring in nearly $40 billion in export
revenue. The smart thing to do is to invest in these job-rich industries, rather than
damage our brand to create a brief fossil fuel bonanza for foreign-owned companies.
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3903
That is why the Greens back clean, sustaina ble farming, and why we back high-value,
environmentally friendly tourism.
The truth is that National’s woeful record  on jobs and job destruction is no accident.
It is happy with high unemployment, because  it helps drive wages down. The Greens
will not put up with it.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I intend raising a point of order myself. Before I call the next
member I have allowed one Government member to read a speech in the general debate.
Having been sucked into that, I had to a llow a member of the Opposition to read a
speech in the general debate. I am sorry for th e rest of the speakers, but in the general
debate this afternoon there will be no more  read speeches. We have had enough of read
speeches.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Your anticipation was brilliant.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. In the
review of the Standing Orders Committee I distinctly recall the discussion and the
agreed version of the repor t that was subsequently re leased. Although there is a
preference for non-read speeches, it was made clear that any member could make—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet. The Speaker does not need a lecture on the
Standing Orders Committee. The Speaker chaired it and remembers it very well. The
exception is for highly technical speeches where Ministers are, for example, introducing
a bill or delivering a speech on the second reading of a bill that may be a technical bill.
But where a member is talking about party politics, the House does not have to suffer
read speeches. Occasionally there is some me rit where perhaps a very humorous speech
has been written out to get the timing, and it can be quite amusing sometimes where a
speech is carefully crafted. But speeches that just climb into party politics are neither
necessarily carefully crafted nor  need to be read by any member in this House, and we
will not have any more this afternoon. The next speaker is the Hon Phil—

items.speaker: Dr Kennedy Graham
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I am still on my feet. I am warni ng the honourable member that this
is a place for debate and we do not need to have speeches written outside of this House
read in this House. Members are meant to come into this House and debate. This is the
general debate. It is not a place to read posit ions of political part ies; it is the general
debate. The House deserves—unless, as I sa y, there are exceptional circumstances—for
members to actually co ntribute to the general debate . That does not involve reading
speeches. I stress that only the Speaker can raise this issue; members are not at liberty to
raise points of order about their colleagues reading speeches.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I respect
your individual recollection of what occurred  in the Standing Orders Committee. That
does not accord with my individual recoll ection of the discussion or the agreed
consensus that emerged in the Standing Orders  review. It is not the case that written
speeches read out would be confined to mi nisterial speeches or technical speeches.
There was some leeway given to individual judgment as to  whether a speech would be
read word for word or used by notes or give n extempore. It was on that basis that the
Green Party—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Maybe it might be of assi stance to the member for me to
read the report of the Standing Orders Committee on this matter.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Do it from memory.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will not attempt to do it from memory. Reading of speeches: “We
also wish to reiterate that, where possibl e, members should not read speeches. The
reading of speeches was precluded until 1996, and we wish to reassert this rule as a
3904 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
convention, rather than through an explicit am endment to the Standing Orders to this
effect. The House is a forum for debate, a nd proceedings are enlivened when members
participate and engage with each other, perhaps with the use of speaking notes to aid the
memory. However, no member, other than th e Speaker, may interrupt the member who
is speaking to suggest a breach of this c onvention, and the Speaker may allow speeches
to be read in some circumstances. Such circumstances may relate to the technical nature
of the material under discussion, or the rela tive experience of the member concerned.
There will, however, be occasions when it is not inappropriate for speeches to be read.”
I think that makes pretty clear what I have  just put to the Hous e, that the Speaker
may accept the reading of speeches where there is technical material, detailed material,
or occasionally where a very cleverly craf ted speech is being delivered. I think all
members can enjoy that from time to time. But a speech presenting a party’s position on
political matters does not need  to be read to this House,  and I have said I acknowledge
that the Hon Chris Finlayson read quite a carefully crafted speech, and on that basis
there was no way I could have intervened in the case of the co-leader of the Green
Party. I have allowed that to happen and all I am saying is that for the rest of the
afternoon, unless I hear a particularly detail ed matter being covered, I expect members
to contribute to the general debate.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You
would recall the very first words you read out in that paragra ph, which says “where
possible”. This accorded an element of indi vidual discretionary j udgment to the MP. It
was on that basis that the Green Party agreed to the report. If you are going to interpret
that paragraph to accord to your self total disc retion as to whether an MP, in his or her
individual judgment, may wish  to make the most boring speech in the annals of this
Parliament, that is not for the Speaker to de termine. If you wish to do that then the
Green Party will revise its view of that report and disassociate itself from it.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I do recall the debate that
occurred at the Standing Orders Committee.  Some of us would have preferred the
wording to be tighter. In fact , some of us promoted having it in the Standing Order as it
had been previously. It was, in the end, a consensus of the committee. The wording
went through without dissent. It had the two exceptions: it was the technical exception
for Ministers, especially on first read ing was the discussion, and, secondly, for
inexperienced members. That member fulfils  neither of those requirements, and I,
therefore, totally support the Speaker’s ruling.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the honourable member. I do not think we need to put
further attention on this this afternoon. It is only for the good of the House that I raise
the issue. I accept that I allo wed one member to read his sp eech this afternoon, and that
is why I wanted to make sure  that on the other side of the House I did not preclude
another member from reading his speech. But I want to encourage members for the rest
of this general debate, which I would rather  we got on with, to please enter into the
spirit of the general debate.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I raise a point of orde r, Mr Speaker. I do not
wish to pursue it beyond this, and this will be my last comm ent on it, but that is not the
understanding on which I participated in—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We are not going to debate  this matter in the House now.
[Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. We are not going to debate this
matter in the House now. The Speaker rules on all matters in this House, and if the
member does not have confidence in the Speaker , there are certain procedures to follow
in that regard. But the Speaker has ruled that, consistent with the findings of the
Standing Orders Committee, there are occasi ons when speeches can be read, indeed. In
fact, I remember on a recent occasion the me mber reading a particularly detailed
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3905
speech, following his attendance at an international conference. I did not intervene in
that case, because there was a lot of detail the member wanted to convey to the House.
That is a judgment of the Speaker. In all matters, the Speaker rules in this House.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: It is very interesting
what is coming from the Green Party in that  view, because what it does is highlight the
points I made this afternoon. I want to tell members what my mother told me. She said:
“Phil, young Phil, when you tell the truth, you never have to remember what you said.”
I say to the Green Party that when you tell the truth, you do not have to read your
speeches. You do not have to gather your lines—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! In saying “you do not have to do this”, and “you do not have
to do that”, the member is referring to  the Speaker. The member must use the
appropriate part of speech, if he is going to attack another party.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I was quoting what my mother  was saying to me, and she
said: “Phil, when you”—Phil—“tell the trut h, you don’t have to remember your lines.
You don’t have to read your sp eeches. We don’t all have to stick to the same line.” The
reality is that over at the Green Party they  are way off beam when  it comes to getting
the facts out there.
There is something we love about Green Party members, and it is that they are
untainted. They are holy, they are pure, and they are untainted. They are untainted by
