reality, they are untainted by experience, and they are untainted by  the facts. I do not
know why the Labour Party is so intent on climbing into bed with them. I find it
interesting that the Labour Party and the Greens are so very much closer together.
The Labour Party said we could not clarify labour laws in order for The Hobbit films
to be made in New Zealand. The Labour Part y hates the hobbits. The Labour Party said
we cannot upgrade roads of national significanc e. In fact, it said “We’re not going to
upgrade the road north of Auckland to Whan garei.” It hates Whangarei people. The
Labour Party said that foreigners cannot i nvest in New Zealand. The irony of that, of
course, is that the Labour Party says it believ es in ethnic diversity. It says “Will people
of different ethnic backgrounds please vote for us—but do not spend your cash in New
Zealand.” The Labour Party said we cannot de liver better public services with fewer
bureaucrats. It said it is ag ainst irrigation in the South Island—and the Labour Party is
against oil and gas exploration, as well.
I would like to present to  the House this map here, because the Labour Party
apparently is against the almost $1 billi on in royalties and company taxes that we
collect each year. This map here shows the ar eas in blue that we have recently released
for block offers across New Zealand—the area s in blue. We are very proud of this. We
hope exploration companies will come here, they will find another M āui gasfield, and
New Zealand will be able to get a little bit of a boost to its local  economy. What this
map also tells you, as the Labour Party rails ag ainst oil and gas exploration, is that the
areas in yellow are what the Labour Party re leased for exploration over the last decade.
[Interruption] Over the last decade the Labour Part y released those areas in yellow for
exploration.
The reason why that is fascinating is that that great statesman of this House, whom
we all love and know, said th is at the time about the release of the Great South Basin
area under Labour Party rule: “Assuming exploration success, the country stands to earn
significant revenue from royalties and taxes flowing from this investment, and it will
assist in ensuring security of energy suppl y.” That great statesman David Parker, the
then Minister of Energy, was very enthus iastic about explori ng in the Great South
Basin. Do you know what? He did it naked. Da vid Parker was naked, because there was
no exclusive economic zone legislation in the Great South Basin when he promoted
that—no regulation out there, at all. The Labour Party believed you could have oil and
3906 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
gas exploration in the Great South Basin without regulation. It turns its back on that
now, because it wants to be greener than green.
Of course, the Labour Party also has forgotten about the M āui gasfield, and all it has
done for 220,000 consumers in the North Island, with New Zealand - made gas. I do not
know why the Labour Party is against such successes. I do not know why it does not
support anything for this country.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I will just straighten my speech notes here, which
have technical details on them. This G overnment believes it can contract out
accountability. It has privatised corrections, it has privatised energy generation, and last
week it pushed through a bill that is going to privatise many of our social welfare
services—

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What did Winston do?

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: —and, what is worse, the Minist er actually promises us there
is even more. There is even more, Mr Be nnett. Look forward to it. New Zealand First
believes that the New Zealand public is actua lly starting to wake up to what the real
agenda of this Government is. The aim of th is Government is to keep its population in a
state of apathy around the economy, with the c ontinual references to “There is no
alternative. We must do this.”, but at the sa me time it is going to privatise the State by
stealth. We can see that in almost every pi ece of legislation that is coming through this
House, but nowhere is it more disturbing than in the field of education.
I am talking about charter schools, and I am  talking about the pr ivatisation of the
State education system, creating an industry for profit, not for our children, not for
academic outcomes, and not for our commun ities. No, no, no—this is an industry for
profit, and those two words prominently appear in the supply and confidence agreement
between this Government and the ACT Pa rty. At the moment it is called charter
schools, but officials quite rightly pointed out in a Cabinet paper, way back in February,
at the beginning of this year, that we alr eady have charter schools here in New Zealand.
Every single State school has a charter, so it has recommended that as early as possible
the working group come up with another name. It has also recommended that a bit of
money be put into actually promoting and putting a bit of spin on this, so that the New
Zealand public think that it is a great id ea that their hard-earned taxpayer education
dollars are given to people who are going to make a profit off it.
The fact that the Government is going to  drop the first two of these schools into
South Auckland and Christchurch in its own disturbing little wa y makes it worse. So
this name is up for grabs. We have got some names. We can all put them in a bucket.
Let us put some forward and add them to those of the working party group. How about:
“Fleece the Taxpayer of Their Education Do llar Schools”. How about that? Shall we
chuck that into the pot, and see whether that—or, what do we say: “We run it up a
flagpole and see if anybody sa lutes.” Is that how you say it, Mr Bennett? What about
“Another of John Banks’ Stupid Ideas Schools”? How would that go? Shall we try that?
We need to get another name, because we already have charter schools. Actually—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: I think she needs to read it.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: None of this is written down, Mr Henare. Some of us actually
can create it on the spot, Mr Henare. These are notes, Mr Henare.
If ever there was a sign that this was a stupid idea, surely it was the flashing sign
above Mr John Banks’ head that this idea cam e out of an ACT Party meeting that was
held in a telephone box. I mean, that is how many people basically voted for, and
participated in, the ACT Party, yet this was th e idea. Or was it? This  is interesting; I
want to quote here, and I wi ll just consult my notes. I am quoting here: “At a meeting
between Mr Banks and a group of education o fficials, Mr Banks wa s quoted as saying:
‘I have outsourced all thinking.’ ” Now, we would suggest—
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3907

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: You had to read that?

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: I wanted to make sure I got it  right, because it is hard to
believe that somebody would say that. But we  would suggest that Mr Banks actually
outsourced his thinking some time before. We would suggest that it is a shame that Mr
Banks did not outsource his memory, because  it would be nice if somebody else could
remember whose helicopter he was on. But he was referring to charter schools and the
working group.
Mr Banks and Mr Key are attempting to sell this charter schools idea, as I said, to the
New Zealand public as a silver bullet. This is the silver bullet for the tail end of our
education system. As I say, they are goi ng to pop it into Sout h Auckland and into
Christchurch. Mr Key has gone  on record as saying: “Thi s is to provide choice.”
Choice! These are the same words the Bush administration used to actually stop central
government investment into the American education system. There are some very
interesting parallels, particularly as our Mi nister of Education s eems to be going to the
United States to do some professional development on it.
But I suggest that we might be being a b it unfair to Mr Banks and the ACT Party.
Perhaps we are crediting them with an idea that actually was not th eirs. Let us look at
the employment of the Secretary for Edu cation, Lesley Longstone. She was actually
appointed in June 2011. That was well befo re the November election. That was well
before any supply and confidence agreemen t, and she has actual ly been hired at
$160,000 more than the person who had the job before her, Karen Sewell, a New
Zealander. Her previous position was actually as a director-general of infrastructure and
funding in the United Kingdom from September 2010, where she was responsible for
delivering free schools. This is privatising, and it is wrong.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: At the risk of sounding sycophantic, I
want to reflect on the National Party’s annual conference, and in particular—
[Interruption] Never, never really, but  I understand the risk. I wa nt to talk  about Phil
Heatley’s speech to the party faithful at  the conference in Auckland on Saturday,
because I think that it was one of the best speeches I have heard one of our Ministers do,
and, in particular, it was about the opportuniti es for oil and gas exploration in this
country. He told the party faith ful a story about a province in this country; a province
that can successfully marry dairying, touris m, and oil and gas exploration completely
comfortably, and has done so for decades. That province—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Lucy Lawless would know that.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: That is right; Lucy Lawless would know exactly
where that is, because that is the province of  Taranaki and the city of New Plymouth. I
think it stands out as the model for what can be done when environmental risks are
managed and when there is a comfortable coalescence with all of those things—
dairying, tourism, and oil and gas. The num bers around Taranaki are quite compelling.
Where New Zealand’s GDP per capita is at around $46,000, Taranaki’s GDP per capita
is at around $88,000. Oil and gas is a significant contributo r to the incr ease over the
national average.
There is another province in this great country of ours, and it has dairying, and it has
great tourism, and it may—just may, subj ect to further exploration—have some
fantastic oil and gas fields not far off its shores.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Canterbury?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: That is the province of Otago—close, Mr Brownlee,
but not quite. In fact, though, it is at the s outh end of the Canterbury Basin, I think they
call it.
I am particularly concerned to ensure th at city leaders in Dunedin are unequivocal
about their support, that as long as envir onmental risk can be managed, that resource
3908 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
should be exploited. So I was a little concerned to read in this morning’s Otago Daily
Times that the Dunedin City Council, fracturin g into two camps, has narrowly decided
to join calls for a moratorium on fracking. Never mind that there is no fracking going on
in Otago, never mind that the Parliamentar y Commissioner for the Environment has not
yet completed her inquiry into the risks of fracking, and certainly never mind that there
was no community consultation before the council passed this motion. It is important,
because I think, as a city leader, that it is time to stand up and say this: as long as the
environmental risks can be managed, Dunedin must promote, must lead, and welcome
the Anadarkos and the Shell Todds who have the exploration licences and head out off
the shore at Karitane and dow n at Nugget Point, and expl ore those fields that Mr
Heatley pointed out.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Not Nugget Point!

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yes, Nugget Point; yes, marine reserve, that is right. It
will be comfortably coalescing, I am sure, with the environment down there, and the
tourism opportunities, and the dairying opportunities in S outh Otago. The three can
coalesce, because the city actually contributed to a mu lti-party economic development
strategy that said: “Dunedin wi ll be one of the world’s great  small cities. It will be
known as a confident, competitive knowledge cen tre,”. It then goes on to talk about
things like business vitality, a compelling destination, a magnet for skills and talent, and
so on. When I was a child—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How about Hillside?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: When I was a child—I will come to that, Dr Clark—
25 percent of the companies listed on the New Zealand Stock Exchange had their head
offices in Dunedin. In the late 1970s and ea rly 1980s there was a flight north and across
the Tasman. That 25 percent—that is righ t, go and have a look at the numbers—the
Donaghys, the Fisher and Paykels, the Shacklo cks, and the McLeods all had their head
offices in Dunedin. I cannot stand by and l ook the people of Dunedin in the eye and say
that it is sad what has happened to Hillside,  that they cannot compete with larger and
more technologically adept companies interna tionally, and then turn  round and say that
we are equivocal about oil and gas exploration. I cannot do it. So I stand up today, and I
say, as a city leader, that I support those companies coming in. They had expertise in
mining, and deep-water mining in particular, an d I think that this w ould be great for the
city. I call on other leaders to do the same, and in particular, the Dunedin City Council.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I am very glad the National Party
members are talking about their so-called gl orious Nuremberg-like rally that happened
on the weekend. The Prime Minister came out of  that, triumphant in his own mind that
the National Party faithful—of course, all of whom who could—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was a completely
unacceptable reference that was made by that member. He should be made to withdraw
and apologise for it. You cannot use words that relate to that particular regime in this
House in other contexts, and it should not be used in the context of this debate when it is
reference to another party as well.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think—

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I withdraw and apologise if any offence was given.

items.speaker: I just say this for the reco rd
items.text: I think the member has got  it completely wrong, but I
withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Had the member referred to something to do with a Nazi-
style conference, that would ha ve been out of or der. I am loath to all the time keep
ruling words out of order. I appreciate the me mber’s preparedness to withdraw it, but I
think we have just got to be careful to not be ruling words out endlessly over the years.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It is not the words; it is the reference he made.
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3909

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member should not be interjecti ng, although I
understand the depth of feeling around some of these issues. The reference is made
through words. I thank the member for withdraw ing his comment, and le t us let it lie at
that. I appreciate that. I thank the member.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: With no link to that, I think the member has gone
troppo, but we will not go there.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not helpful.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: He had a bad day yesterday. We have it now in
writing from a High Court judge confirmi ng what everybody knows in Canterbury and
around the place, that Gerry Brownlee is incomp etent, and we now have the papers to
prove it. But let us go back to the great ra lly of the National Part y conference. Out of
that came the Prime Minister, and he announced a loyalty scheme as part of one of the
biggest wealth transfers in our history—w hich I suspect we will look back on it as—
from those who cannot afford it to those w ho can. He came into this House with a
loyalty scheme that is an admission of defeat , because if the Prime Minister felt, as he
has trumpeted, as Gerry Brownlee has, and as all the National Party members have, that
these shares in our assets will be retained almost ad infinitum in the future by ordinary
Kiwi mums and dads, then the question re mains why you need a loyalty scheme, and
why that loyalty scheme will be paid on th e back of all those who cannot afford the
$1,000 to $2,000 parcels.
The Prime Minister then came into the House yesterday, from my memory—I note
this for the press gallery, because when we would get up in the House from time to time
when we were in Government, the press galle ry, as were the then Opposition, were at
pains to ask us to provide detail around costings and other things—he got up and was
asked for detail around the loyalty scheme. Zero; he had not thought it through. He was
asked for a costing around the loyalty scheme. Zero; he did not have the numbers. Then
he decided to criticise this si de of the House for references  to an authoritative Treasury
report, from his own Government departme nt, but could not put a dollar figure on the
costings, a dollar figure on the impact, no detail,  and no reference at all. There are those
in the media who would term that, perhaps, as “policy on the hoof”. That term, I think,
is too light for this.
The Prime Minister on radio called me a fool for references I made around State-
owned enterprises. Well, I say this to th e Prime Minister: only a fool would swap
revenue-generating assets making around 18 pe rcent for debt-servicing costs of around
5 percent, and every Kiwi who can bala nce their housekeeping and make the budget
work every day has worked that out. The fool  is the Prime Minister. The fool is the
Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister has tried to say benevolently to people who
already own the assets that they can buy those assets back for a second time—for a
second time, because we know that they already own them. Then he said to them that
those who do buy in, those who can afford  $1,000 or $2,000—and if they can, ordinary
Kiwis, I suspect, will pay off 20 percent of th e credit card rather than invest in this—
will get a loyalty bonus. Those who cannot afford it get nothing.
Then, of course, we have  the issue of possible M āori tribal and iwi challenges. Yet
the Prime Minister and his ilk go ahea d, bludgeon this thr ough—bludgeon an initial
public offering through under the worst market  conditions you can possibly have and
under the potential threat of le gal action. I ask how that will be resolved. That will be
resolved, of course, in the tried and true way of the Prime Mini ster making a deal. I
suspect that it will be resolved through a share allocation. So we have a bonus share
allocation. Kiwis are so loyal that they do not need it, but the Prime Minister has thrown
it in. By the way, that bonus matures—hey presto—in about 3 years’ time. When is that,
colleagues? Just after the next  election. I ask National, given that it has not made up its
3910 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
mind on much, whether it will guarantee that th at bonus issue, that loyalty scheme, will
mature prior to the next election—prior to the next election, say, in 2½ years’ time. That
is a bribe and a con, designed simply so the Prime Minister can say that all Kiwis are
in—until they get the windfall bonus in the lead-up to an  election, and then we know
Kiwis will be out, and foreign investors will be the ones who are in.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker.
Tēnā tātou e te Whare. I am really interested in young people, and at a recent motivation
event I heard the principle of “Be. Do. Get.” The principle behind that is the idea that
intrinsically you are worth valu e, but unless you “do”, you do not get the results that
you deserve. The National Government understands  that all too well. Contrary to what
Mr Cosgrove said, we are an intelligent G overnment, we are work ing hard, and we are
action-packed. You will hear from my othe r colleagues the activities that we are
involved in. But what we understand is that it is OK to be the Government, but you have
to “do” if you want to get the future that New Zealanders need, want, and deserve.
As the MP for Christchurch Central, to me the most important commitment this
Government has made is to support the rebui ld and the recovery of Christchurch and
Canterbury, and this Government is 100 pe rcent behind that. Those of you who have
visited Canterbury or Christchurch will know that we are totally focused on the
earthquake recovery. In fact, I do not know what  we did or what we talked about before
the earthquakes. We worked t ogether really well to manage  the disaster, and we are
working together well to manage the recover y. But things are still tough. There are still
difficult, challenging issues out there, but we are making progress. We are focusing on
fixing homes because we want everybody safe and warm. We have worked on resettling
people who had totally damaged properties,  and 5,000 of the 7,000-ish who have been
in the red zone have now signed their documents and are ready to move on. We have
also repaired 20,000 houses. That is a little bit bigger than the size of Timaru. There are
still 30,000 houses in that proce ss, but we have also put accommodation villages there
so people can move out of their houses, m ove into that accommodation, and then move
back into their house s when they are finished. The good news is that Fletcher EQR—
that is, the earthquake recovery people—are  telling us that they are completing 100 a
day.
We are getting very good at demolition. We have demolished about 1,200
commercial buildings in the centre city, w ith another 200 to go. That might sound
negative, but in actual fact it is really positive. You ca nnot rebuild until those buildings
are down. And we are rebuilding fast, as well. The stadium was up in 100 days. The
new out-patients department at Christchurch Hospital was up in 150 days. And our new
library has just opened this week. So we are trying to fix communities. It is actually
horrifying the number of public and community  buildings that are being repaired or
coming down. We are also fixing infrastructure: the roads, the pipes, the sewers—things
that you cannot see too much, but  things that are incredibly important. I have some
statistics here: 41,000 square metres of roading, 1,500 kilometres of water network
assessed, and 45 kilometres re paired. Overall, there ar e 200 projects going on in
Christchurch worth over $920 million. So if you get the feeling that there are roadworks
going on in every street in town, you are probably right.
But it is not just building infrastructure th at is important; we also need to focus on
the health and well-being of Cantabrians. I really want to c ongratulate the health
professionals in Christchurch, who under ve ry difficult circumstances with really
broken facilities have delivered first-class health. What is more, they are now dealing
with the normal winter ills in the city  as well. In terms of well-being, I think
Cantabrians are amazing. They are resilient, they are positive, and they are working
hard to rebuild our city. Our economy is growing, new businesses are opening and old
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3911
businesses reopening every day,  unemployment is down, and there are people actually
moving to Christchurch to be part of the re building. We are very pl eased with the local
plans that are under way, and we are lookin g forward to the central Christchurch
blueprint, which will be announced next Monday. I have absolutely no doubt that
Cantabrians can and will rebuild a better, st ronger, and more environmentally friendly
and beautiful city. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: It is very clear that this Government has a
propensity to appoint its friends in order to advance its own interests. It does not matter
whether it is Brian Neeson, Ken Shirley, Ra vi Musuku, Georgina te Heuheu, Sir Wira
Gardiner, Wayne Mapp, Jenny Shipley, Stev en McElrea, Judy Kirk, Don Brash,
Richard Griffin, or Richard Long, and I could go on with an assortment of former
members of Parliament, electorate chairpeo ple, failed candidates for the National Party,
or old staffers. This Government continue s to appoint people it prefers in order to
advance its own interests.
There is one particular appoi ntment that I want to sp eak about with some real
seriousness, because it goes to just what th e Government is trying to achieve with its
appointments. One of the people in the last manifestation of the National caucus whom I
admired a great deal was Katherine Rich. She is a woman of ability and principle, and I
admired her a great deal. She, in fact, led the National caucus on some issues, such as
the section 59 debate, when she refused to be whipped and follow the party line, and
made sure that we got better legislation than was in place. This is a person of principle,
Katherine Rich, and she is the head of th e Food and Grocery Council. So why has the
Government appointed her to the Health Prom otion Agency? There is clearly a conflict
of interest.
The food and beverage industry is a $15 b illion industry, and the Food and Grocery
Council’s own objective is “To promote, oppos e, or move for the recision of any
legislation, regulations, by-laws , or policy affecting the inte rests of members.”, and I
quote that from the objectives of the New Z ealand Food and Grocery Council. My very
great fear is that they have deliberately created this conflict of interest for a woman of
ability because they wish to have some m itigating influence on the work of the Health
Promotion Agency. What is the objective of  the Health Promotion Agency? Well, the
Health Promotion Agency, it says, “must l ead and support activities for the following
purposes: (a) promoting health and … encour aging health lifestyles: (b) preventing
disease, illness, and injury: (c) enabling environments that support health and … healthy
lifestyles:”. The Food and Grocery Counc il has campaigned against the mandatory
inclusion of folic acid in bread, it has campaigned against the reduction of salt and sugar
in food, and it has campaigned in favour of liberal trading policies for alcohol.
So my distinct suspicion is that this Government has cynically appointed this woman
of ability so that it can mitigate messages th at should come out of the Health Promotion
Agency, so that nobody could ever accuse it of  being nanny State, and so that it can
reassure its friends in the f ood and grocery industry that it still has their interests at
heart. “Do not worry, we will not let any of  that namby-pamby health promotion stuff
get away on us. We will make sure that we do not do anything that affects the sale of
your sugary products, or your salt-laden pr oducts, or your products that do not inspire
health or healthy living in any New Zealander.”
My very deep concern is that National’s cronyism not only sacrifices some of its best
people but also is used in the interests of the industries that support it. In this particular
case, its cronyism is used against the inte rests of the health and well-being of New
Zealanders. This is one conflict of interest that this Government is using deliberately for
its own purposes, and it needs to reflect seriously on that issue. Thank you.
3912 General Debate 25 Jul 2012

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Today we were very privileged in
this House to have the presence of the Prime Minister of Zi mbabwe, a man who has
made a huge commitment to his country and is  a leader of his region. He has, I guess,
had to eat a few bitter pills in his time to actually deliver what he wants to see for his
country going forward. But that is a true  leader: somebody who knows what their
country wants, who is willing to do what is  needed for their country, and who has the
presence and ability to deliver that over time. We wish him the best in those
endeavours. Just like the New Zealand Nati onal Party is a part y that has the best
interests of New Zealand at heart, that is making the right choices for New Zealand, and
that is willing and able to go through the tough times to make those choices a reality and
to make this country good and great. We are lucky to have the leadership of this country
in the hands of National at this time.
The Labour Party has no plan. It attacks pe rsonalities. That last speech from the Hon
Maryan Street was very disappo inting in the way that it tr ied to attack a personality,
rather than to go and to look at the real future of New Z ealand and to put a plan out
there. It is very divisive po litics that you see from the Oppo sition. It tries to prey on the
fears of individuals, it tries to prey on those who are w eak, and it tries to make
something out of nothing so that it can actua lly go out there and be seen as the saviour
of all when it is not the saviour at all. It is not the saviour. It do es not believe in New
Zealanders or in this country. It believes only in itself and in the grand conspiracy
theories that you see from parties like the Ne w Zealand First Party in this House this
afternoon, whereas on the National Government side, we know what we need to do. We
need to have a balanced economy; an ec onomy that has the f undamentals right; an
economy that invests in those very strong prin ciples of education, infrastructure, and
development—
Denis O’Rourke: An economy that widens the gap between rich and poor.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: —an economy that looks after people in need; and an economy
that delivers for all. And when we hear members across there trying to yell out things
from the Opposition benches, they do not l ook at what is actually required for New
Zealand. We hear this in regard to the mixed-ownership model. The Opposition and
Grant Robertson started off today saying it is a transfer of wealth. That is what he is
saying. Well, it is not a tran sfer of wealth. The people who will potentially buy those
assets through the shareholdings are actua lly sending money to the Government for
those shares. The Government will benefit from  that investment; that investment then
will be used to deliver more  public services for all New Zealanders. If anything, the
transfer of wealth is from those who are wi lling to invest, to the Government to deliver
for all New Zealanders. That is what is really going to happe n, rather than a transfer of
wealth, as the Labour Party seeks to assert in this House.
I thought we had a very good speech today fr om Chris Finlayson, though. It was an
excellent speech, and it followed his excellent  debate at the National Party conference.
He spoke about the change in how the leadership of the Labour Party is determined and
said that it has inevitably meant that Mr Sh earer has got a prolonged stage of leadership
of the Labour Party, which is good news fo r National, and it is good news for New
Zealand because Mr Shearer will not achieve his goal of being Prime Minister. That will
mean that National has more opportunity at the next election with him as the Labour
Party leader.
When you look at the Green Party, though, it is very disappointing what it is doing in
this House and in the public eye. The Green Party should be a party that talks about the
real issues. The Green Party is  a party that should look at the truth and de liver that in
this House. The Green Party does not do that. The Green Party is a party at odds with its
coalition favourites, the Labour Party. They naturally will be at odds, because the
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3913
Labour Party does not want to lose votes to  the Greens and the Gr eens want to take
votes off the Labour Party. That is a marriag e that cannot last. There will be some
divisive fighting between those two parties in  the next 2 years as  they fight over the
same territory. The Labour Party has one a dvantage over the Green Party, and it is that
it tells the truth more often than the Green  Party—not that much more, but it does
sometimes. That is one thing that the Green Pa rty needs to invest in if it seriously wants
votes.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: E te Māngai o te Whare, t ēnā koe. The speech from the
last speaker, “Mr Ardern”, talked about tel ling the truth. I will tell the truth about what
this Government is doing with our natural asse ts as well as our State-owned assets. Just
as it is selling off our State-owned energy companies, the Government is selling off and
trading away our natural assets, and I am talking to two particular proposals in Te
Wāhipounamu - South West New Zealand Worl d Heritage Area. It is Riverstone
Holdings’ proposed monorail and Milford Da rt’s proposed tunnel between Glenorchy
and the Hollyford. I am very pleased the Mini ster of Conservation is here, because she
recently received some of the concerns of the people of Te Ānau that that proposal for
the tunnel would completely unde rmine tourism in the area. It would take people away
from visiting Te Ānau.
These two proposals are proposed for one of our most distinctive and special natural
areas: the wilds of Fiordland, of Snowdon Forest. They are both part of Te
Wāhipounamu - South West New Zealand World Heritage Area. It is one of only 188
areas that are recognised by Unesco for their outstanding value to all humankind.
Earlier this year I walked through the Kiwi Burn and the Ūpukerora valleys, where
the monorail is proposed to go. The trees and th e forest in those valleys—it is red beech
forest. There are some very beautiful trees; some very old trees that are potentially
hundreds and hundreds of years old. The m onorail would create a 200 metre wide, 30
kilometre long scar through th e Snowdon Forest. By the Department of Conservation’s
own estimates it would destroy 20,000 trees , which would have to be logged and
cleared to create the corridor for the monorail.
Riverstone Holdings is targeting conservation land because, of course, it is much
cheaper to socialise its costs by using public conservation land for fr ee or for a modest
concession, rather than buying private la nd for its proposed monorail. Yet the
Department of Conservation is supposed to be managing these areas for the preservation
and protection of the natural resources that ar e there. It is the habitat of threatened
species like k ākā, k ākāriki, and the long-tailed bat, ye t Riverstone Holdings proposes
putting people in these sealed tin cans to send them swishing through the landscape.
How will that increase their appreciation of  what a New Zealand forest is like? By
cutting the journey between Queenstown and Te Ānau and missing out that beautiful
section round the lake, where the road is in  the shadow of the Remarkables and you are
looking out across Lake Wakatipu, how will that increase people’s appreciation of New
Zealand?
It goes through an area that at the moment is perfect for families and novice trampers
because it is close to the Mavora Lakes. Se nsible tourism operators, people whom the
Green Party supports and who are establishing the Save Fiordland So ciety, see that the
future of that industry is based on getting people into  the outdoors and encouraging
them to see what nature is really like, not just to have them speeding through the
landscape in a sealed tin can. Those operators  are part of the Save Fiordland Society.
Those people are banding together to mobilis e public opinion against these two very
destructive, high-impact proposals.
We have not had a good record from this Minister. She presided over the freeholding
of part of what was to be part of Craigieb urn Forest Park, and a llowed it to be traded
3914 General Debate 25 Jul 2012
and sold off to the Porters Ski Area development. Mr Michael Slee, who was the
director of development for the Porters Sk i Area proposal, is al so involved in the
monorail proposal. Once they had their conce ssions from the Minist er, what happened?
Blackfish, which was involved in putting forw ard Porters Ski Area, was onsold to four
Russian multimillionaires. Given the large amount of capital that is required for both the
tunnel and the monorail, what would we se e here? We would see overseas corporates
that might benefit from the jobs and the c onsultancy contracts involved in constructing
the monorail and the tunnel, but these woul d be overseas-owned companies destroying
New Zealand nature in return for their dividends going offshore.
People are mobilising to stop these proposal s in order to protect the outstanding
values of the South West New Zealand Worl d Heritage Area, because they recognise
that this is conservation land.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal. Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I
am starting my contributi on by greeting you in the M āori language, because this is the
week when we are acknowledging the M āori language. If we want  to keep our culture
alive we need to stick to our language, and that is very important. English is not my first
language, and you had a little debate today that debaters should not read their speeches.
I read my speech because of this House’s prestige. I do not want to get stuck
somewhere. That is why I prepare my notes , my thoughts, so that I can keep reading
them. Mr Speaker, I hope you will excuse me if I read in between my speech some of
my notes. I am not used to debating without my notes.
When we migrants come to this country, we bring a lot of dreams in mind. We have
got a lot of energy for the hard work that we are ready to do, and we are sure we will
succeed with the hard work and support of our families. I am proud to be part of this
National Government, which provides the tool s for businesses to gr ow in this country.
Less red tape-ism, better infrastructure, and better facilities are the success tools for
businesses to grow. I am sure everyone fr om the small and medium-sized businesses
will agree with me that the National Government is supporting them.
I am proud of this National-led Government, which gave this country its first ethnic
MP, Pansy Wong. I am also proud of this Government, which gave us Pansy Wong as
the first Cabinet Minister from an ethnic b ackground. I am proud to be part of this team
and I hope this Government will keep on working in this direction.
I would like to quote Mahatma Gandhi, who said: “Men often become what they
believe themselves to be. If I believe I cannot do something, it makes me incapable of
doing it. But when I believe I can, then I acquire  the ability to do it even if I didn’t have
it in the beginning.” It is very important that  the businesses, which are run with a lot of
hard work and the support of the families, succeed over here. What every business that
starts needs is a great idea to start with, resources and capital to succeed, a workforce
that can help it to produce its production, and, lastly, infrastructure so that it can sell its
product not only in this country but also ov erseas. The Government for its part is
supporting facilities and multiple initiatives, be cause it is our sincere wish to see that
everyone living in New Zealand should succeed.
We are also involved in a number of initiati ves that facilitate the growth of ethnic
businesses. The forums organi sed by the ethnic affairs mini stry are directed to help
them to succeed over here. The recent forum organised by the ethnic affairs ministry
about the African community was very successful. Ther e the Minister for Ethnic
Affairs, the Hon Judith Collins, said that New Zealand’s African community brings
with it a great deal of energy and experience to our shores, and we are able to use that
experience and energy in the development of this country.
I feel that organising such events is a wonderful way to empower individuals and
communities. It makes them feel welcome a nd says to them: “We are there to support
25 Jul 2012 General Debate 3915
you while you are integrating into New Zealand.” It provi des migrants coming to New
Zealand with a sense that now they belong to New Zealand, and their efforts towards
building the New Zealand economy will be well supported.
I would like to finish by saying another quote by Mahatma Gandhi: “As human
beings, our greatness lies not so much in be ing able to remake the world … as being
able to remake ourselves.” This, I believe, is the story of most migrants. T ēnā koe, Mr
Speaker.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
HOLIDAYS (FULL RECOGNITION OF WAITANGI DAY AND ANZAC DAY)
First Reading
Debate resumed from 27 June.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : I certainly want to use my final 2 minutes for the
purpose of recording that New Zeala nd First does support the Holidays (Full
Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day)  Amendment Bill, and there are five
reasons to do so.
One is the opportunity for observance by all employees, and that should be
something that is primary in the considera tion of the bill. Without the opportunity to
observe these important days, we do not have a proper system of observance at all. The
second reason relates to fairness. Some empl oyees work on weekend days and some do
not. It should be fair between them all. The third relates to consistency. There should be
more consistency around which days you can Mondayise and which you cannot.
Fourthly, we need to enhance the importance of these two days. And, fifthly, there is no
real burden on the economy from doing so.
Finally, as a holiday can be granted in tw o out of seven years on average, there can
be no burden on employers either.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: May I begin by saying that we on this side
of the House are voting against the Holid ays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and
ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. I want to us e the time I have available to actually
explain to the other side what I seen as lacking.
There is, obviously, a lack of understanding  on the other side of the House, on the
Opposition benches, of the primary industries, which we are very fortunate to have. The
effects of such legislation on the primary i ndustries has been perverse for some time.
The whole exercise and example around this can be illustrated well by looking at Anzac
Day, should it fall on a weekend. There are many employers and employees who are
involved in flexible working situations. I want to use one that is fairly close to my heart,
and that is the wool industry. In regard to  the shearing industry, it is not uncommon to
be in a situation where workers these days  are managing farms. When it comes down to
actually trying to get some cohesion and coordination within a seasonal pressure
situation, such events as are being proposed by this bill are nothing but cumbersome and
obstructive.
An example is a farming business where the employer enforces the employees
getting the sheep in ready for a Monday start or a Tuesday start. In the event of this bill,
what happens? It is a Wednesday start. So th ere are costs. This is just one example.
There is the other situation where there are very often wet seasonal situations. A
situation comes down to its Friday and it has been raining for a week, then in the
weekend it comes right. Nobody is going to st art work on Sunday, because there is
another holiday on Monday. Nobody starts work until Wednesday. We are talking about
3916 Holidays (Waitangi & ANZAC Days) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
thousands of people who are affected by this  situation. Weather-dependent situations do
arise. Whether it is making of silage, maki ng of hay, or putting in the critical winter
crop, it is guided by a situation. We are not talking abou t 1 day or 2 days  here; we are
talking about 4 days, in effect. I have seen no indication of consider ation of that from
the other side of the House.
In effect, this sort of legislation also creates inequity around th e business model that
is operating at the time. It enables an owner-operator to carry on doing their thing,
whereas an employer, who offers job secu rity to employees, is totally put at
disadvantage. What these sorts of bills do is actually create perverse incentives whereby
the employer will put employees on subcontracti ng situations to be able to get round
this situation.
You may say on the other side of the Hous e that 88 percent of people come from
urban areas and only 12 percent of people from rura l areas. Well, that is not quite the
case.
I can say with great pride that it never happened in my day—and thank goodness it
did not—and it should not be happening today. When we look at work, the popular view
is that a holiday is marvellous, but from my own personal experi ence a holiday with
four children was a costly expe rience. When you look at the fa mily situation today, it is
quite clear that this bill is making a rath er complex employment situation even more
complex.
It is objectionable that people on the other side of the House, in Opposition, stand in
the way of people who want to work. It is sort of consistent, when you stop and think
about it, because the Opposition finds it better to give away productivity—better to give
away those opportunities for New Zealand to get ahead. On the National Party side of
things here, we are very proud of the work we  have done to try to make sure that this
economy grows and goes ahead.
Let us count some of those things. The complexity of this bill does not address the
full situation. In the hospitality area, a lot of people have Mondays off. They work from
Tuesday to Saturday and they will not be cove red. So as far as this bill addressing an
anomaly, all it does is create further comple xity. Within the primary sector there are
some huge problems around the complexity. Today, as in my day, when the sheep are
dry or when the hay is ready to be made, that is when you should work. So I have no
difficulty in opposing this bill.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: What an extraordinary speech
from Colin King! I think somewhere in the mi ddle of that speech he decided he did not
like Christmas, he did not seem to particular ly like children very much either, and he
does not want people to have holidays. Bu t the National Party, unfortunately, has a
history—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: He’s got children.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Yes, he has. That is right, Mr Guy—he has. And the point
of that interjection is? The National Party has never liked the idea of workers getting
holidays. It has never liked it. When legisl ation on 4 weeks’ annual leave came to this
House the National Party members got up and they opposed it. Judith Collins said this
during the debate on 4 weeks’ leave: “I do not have a lo t of sympathy with anyone who
wishes to be generous,”. That is what Judith  Collins said when she got up in this House
to debate 4 weeks’ annual leave. The sky did not fall in when the Labour-led
Government introduced 4 weeks’  annual leave. In fact, peop le got to spend more time
with their families, and they got to enjoy more time in their communities.
Holidays for workers are actually very impor tant for productivit y, and that is why
businesses actually support this legislati on, the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi
Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. Busine sses know that in 5 out of 7 years they
25 Jul 2012 Holidays (Waitangi & ANZAC Days) Amdt Bill 3917
will have to plan to give people time off fo r Waitangi Day and Anzac Day. It is not that
difficult to turn that into 7 out of 7 years.  That is what businesses are saying. Today in
the House we have already heard that Ma rtin Snedden from the Tourism Industry
Association is saying that this is great—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: A great New Zealander.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: He is a great New Zealande r who supports a great bill,
because what he said is that  this is going to be good for the economy. This is actually
going to lead to more business on those days that people have a holiday.
But, ultimately, this bill is about a fa ir deal for families in New Zealand. The
Holidays Act has 11 public holidays in it and in every year New Zealanders deserve a
fair go to have those 11 pub lic holidays. It is an anom aly that when Anzac Day and
Waitangi Day fall on a weekend we do not create a holiday on a Monday. It happens for
Christmas Day. We hear from people on the ot her side of the House that somehow or
other this very good bill is diminishing the importance of Anzac Day and Waitangi Day.
Far, far from it: Christmas Day, when it fa lls on a weekend, generates a holiday on a
Monday. Has Christmas suddenly lost its importance in New Zealand? Absolutely not.
Anzac Day and Waitangi Day are important days in New Zealand’s history. They are
an important part of our identity. This bill will enable New Zealanders to commemorate
those days on the days they fall, on 6 Fe bruary and 25 April, and it will give New
Zealanders the days off every year—not just  for 5 years in 7. That is a good thing. In
Australia, where in most states this applie s, attendance at Anzac Day services has been
going up. People value the day, they value th e importance of the day to our national
identity, and they also enjoy the fact that they can have a day off with their families.
This bill has been a long time coming, a nd, as someone in whose name it formerly
was, I can tell you that  it is enormously popular with New Zealanders. New Zealanders
understand that they deserve a fair deal. Ne w Zealanders work hard. New Zealanders
work harder than most people around th e world, and that is a good thing. But New
Zealanders deserve the 11 public  holidays in the Holidays Act every year. This bill is a
bill that the Labour Party is in credibly proud to bring to this House because it is about
fairness for families. It is about a fair deal  so that people can actually spend more time
with their families. Why would National oppos e a fair deal for families? Why would
National say that workers do not deserve the 11 public holidays that they are guaranteed
every year in the Holidays Act?
I believe that Waitangi Day and Anzac Day wi ll continue to grow in importance for
New Zealanders. They will continue to be part of what shapes our national identity.
What this bill does is recognise the im portance of those days and says to New
Zealanders that they will get a fair deal. That is the fair deal that a Labour Government
will provide. In Opposition we are at least able to put this bill forward. I am very
grateful for the support from other parties, wh ich I am sure will see this bill pass, and it
will be a great day for New Zealand families.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora t ātau katoa. I a t ātau e k ōrero nei m ō tenei o ng ā pire, e rua ng ā take nui
whakaharahara, e p īrangitia nei e au, e m ātau o te P āti Māori hei whakatakoto ki mua i
te aroaro o te Whare P āremata. Tuatahi ko t ērā o ng ā waiata, ng ā karanga nei me k ī,
“honour the Treaty”, t ērā kōrero. Ka rua, ko te āhuatanga o te waihotanga mai o T ā
Apirana Ngata i te wā i a ia. Arā, ko tana kōrero, ko “the price of citizenship”. Ēnei take
katoa, “honour the Treaty”, “the pr ice of citizenship”,  kei reira tonu t ētahi hononga ki
waenganui i ngā kaupapa e rua i roto i tēnei pire.
Ehara i te mea kua aro atu m ātau ki t ēnei mea ko te hararei, k āo. Kua waihotia ake
tērā ki te taha. Ehara i te  mea kua aro atu ki te āhuatanga o tēnei mea o te moni, me ng ā
mahi o te pakihi, k āo. Ka waiho t ērā ki reira. Kotahi tonu te kaupapa, ko t ō tātau
3918 Holidays (Waitangi & ANZAC Days) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
nohotahi, i raro i te korowai o Aotearoa. Ngā rā e 2, kātahi nei ngā rā whakaharahara hei
hanga i tēnei mea ko te kotahitanga o Aotearoa. Ka mutu, ko t ā tātau nohotahi ā-Māori,
ā-Pākehā me kī i te whenua kotahi. Me pēnā ka tika i tēnei rā, i tēnei wiki i te mea ko Te
Wiki o Te Reo Māori tēnei, 25 tau mai i te w ā i whakamanahia ai te rā o Te Reo Māori.
Me kī ko te ture Maori Language Act 1987.
Ko ēnei momo ture, me t ērā o te Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, he kaupapa nui
whakaharahara o roto i a t ātau. Nā runga i te aha n ā runga i te mea ko ēnei kaupapa e
rua, e hangaia nei hei whakakotahi nei i a t ātau—kaua ki te whakawehewehe. Ka mutu,
ka puta te k ōrero he whenua motuhake a Aotearoa, t ā tātau noho ā-iwi Tiriti, ā-iwi
tangata whenua.
Ko ētahi o te motu ka k ī atu, ē, nō mua noa atu, n ō ngā rā ō nehe ēnei kōrero katoa.
Waiho ngā take o te Tiriti o Waitangi ki mua,  ki reira tahuna mai ai. Ka mutu, k āre he
paku pānga o ērā kaupapa o ng ā tau 1840. Waiho ērā ki reira k āre he take o ēnei rā, ko
tāku ko te k ī atu e k āo, kāo. Me kōrero i ēnei kōrero mō te Tiriti ka tahi, me k ōrero mō
te āhuatanga o te hunga i haere ki t āwāhi mō te pakanga. Ka mutu kei reira tonu t ētahi
tauira ō roto i te Muriwhenua fishing report i te tau 1988. Ka puta te k ōrero a te
Taraipiunara o Waitangi, mō te āhuatanga o te Tiriti o Waitangi i ēnei rā. Anei tā rātau i
te reo Pākehā: “Any impracticality today results not from the Treaty but from our failure
to heed its terms. The important point is that there was, and still is, room for an
agreement to be made.” He kupu whakaharahara ēnei kupu i te mea, he mea
whakaohooho nei i te āhuatanga o te tīmatanga mai o te Tiriti. Ka mutu, he hononga o te
Tiriti Pākehā ki te Ao Māori e noho nei i raro i te kor owai kotahi. Me maumahara an ō
hoki tātau, i hainatia te Tiriti i te tau 1840. Ka mutu, 200,000 M āori ki t ērā o te 2,000
Pākehā. Ko wai te pōrangi ka kī atu ka tukuna e te Māori tōna rangatiratanga ki te hunga
manuhiri me kī. Kāre au i te whakaae atu ki tērā. Nō reira, i whai atu ngā mātua tīpuna o
te Ao M āori i t ēnei huarahi kia nohotahi i raro i te āhuatanga o t ēnei mea o te
rangatiratanga kua mōhio tonu tātau e noho taupatupatu ngā kaupapa.
Ka mutu, ka hoki mai ki te āhuatanga o te Anzac. He kaupapa an ō rā tērā kua pā mai
ki a t ātau. I te rau tau kua hipa ake, i konei a T ā Apirana Ngata, i roto i t ēnei Whare
Pāremata, i mua o te w ā o te haerenga o ng ā hōia ki t āwāhi, me tana k ōrero mō tēnei
mea o “the price of citizenship”. Ko tana k ōrero, i haere ng ā Māori ki t āwāhi ki te
pakanga i tuku i te āhuatanga o t ēnei mea o te oranga o te tangata m ō te aha? Ka mutu
mō te equal citizenship i raro i te korowai o te Tiriti o Waitangi.
Nō reira ēnei kōrero katoa e h āngai tonu ana ki a t ātau ināiatonunei. Nō reira koinei
te āhuatanga o t ā mātau harikoa kua eke t ēnei o ng ā kōrero ki mua i te aroaro o te
Whare Pāremata. Ko tā te Pāti Māori he tautoko i te ia o t ēnei pire, ka mutu ka tautoko
ake kia taea ai e te marea, te w ānanga te hōhonutanga o tēnei mea, kia hoki mai ki taku
kōrero, e rua ngā take, “honour the Treaty” ka tahi, “the price of citizenship” ka rua. Ērā
atu kōrero katoa mō te moni, waiho mō te wā. Tēnā koutou, kia ora tātau.
[Greetings, Mr Speaker. Greetings, everyone. As  we debate this bill there are two
concepts that we, the M āori Party, wish to present befo re Parliament. Firstly, there is
the activist chant “honour the Treaty”, and, secondly, there is the legacy of Sir Apirana
Ngata’s phrase “the price of citizenship”. Both are connected intimately in this bill.
Our support is not connected to the opportuni ty for a holiday. Neither is it about the
impact of this bill on productivity or whether Mondayising the day makes good business
sense. Our support is founded on the fundamental importance of these 2 days in helping
define our sense of nationhood. Of course, it is  an appropriate time to be doing this, in
Māori Language Week, the 25th anniversary of the Maori Language Act 1987.
Legislation like that Act and the 1975 Treaty of Waitang i Act are milestones along
the way in the journey of nation-building. They are pointers in our collective knowledge
25 Jul 2012 Holidays (Waitangi & ANZAC Days) Amdt Bill 3919
about what makes us unique: the relationship between the indigenous people, the people
of the Treaty.
Some people seem to speak of history—more particularly, the events of 1840, or the
world wars in which our nation served—as be ing about a past that has no relevance to
today. I reject those sentiments. That is precisely why we need to continue to talk about
the Treaty and to reflect on those who went overseas to war. In the Muriwhenua fishing
report of 1988, the Waitangi Tribunal spo ke about the practical application of the
Treaty for the modern world. This is what they had to say in English: “Any
impracticality today results not  from the Treaty but from our  failure to heed its terms.
The important point is that there was, and s till is, room for an agreement to be made.”
These words are important because they remind us  that at the genesis of the Treaty was
a solemn commitment for two parties to live together. We have to remember that when
the Treaty was signed in 1840, the population was something like 200,000 M āori and
2,000 P ākehā. It does not make sense that those chiefs who signed the Treaty would
voluntarily give up power to a visitor, so to speak. Our M āori ancestors pursued this
pathway to ensure the continuation of Māori authority, which continues to be debated.
Let me return to Anzac Day, which is very significant to us. Last century in
Parliament Sir Apirana Ngata de scribed the participation of M āori in the war effort as
“the price of citizenship”. Hi s enduring battle cry was that M āori sacrifice and service
in the name of war should be honoured with the recognition of full and equal citizenship
as promised in the Treaty of Waitangi.
And so all of these statements pertain to us now. Therefore, we are delighted this
debate is before Parliament. The M āori Party endorses the essence of this bill and we
support the public delving into the complex asp ects of this matter as I repeat two calls:
“honour the Treaty” and “the price of citi zenship”. Leave the debate about money for
another time. Thank you.]

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora
koutou, and kia ora to that member, Te Urur oa Flavell. I want to take members’
memories back to earlier this year when we  enjoyed fine weather across the country on
both Waitangi Day and Anzac Day. We had record crowds around the country
commemorating those events and people spending time with their families, friends, and
loved ones. But the year before last, and last year, people mi ssed out on their full
complement of holidays. This year, by c ontrast, we had increased commemorations and
increased celebrations. I am looking forward to  this bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition
of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill, passing through the House so that
hard-working Kiwis can get the holidays they deserve every year, not just in 5 years out
of 7.
I want to acknowledge again at this point  the contribution of Grant Robertson, who
originally drafted this bill. His astuteness ne eds to be put on the record. I have been
proud to sponsor this bill, because it is a good bill. It is a bill th at is about a fair deal for
Kiwi families. There are 11 public holidays in the Holidays Act, and we deserve all 11.
This bill makes sure we get them all. Th e growing significance of Waitangi Day and
Anzac Day to our sense of history and identity as New Zealanders means that they
deserve full recognition—full recognition, in th e same way that other holidays get full
recognition.
I want to take a minute just to contemplate what we have heard from the other side of
the House in this debate. The strongest argum ent, perhaps, if we could call it that, has
been put forward by David Bennett, who an nounced that we should not fix this
problem, because it does not happen again for a while. I want to suggest that that is akin
to not fixing the roof because it is not raini ng. The problem is here  in front of us. We
have the opportunity to fix it, and we should get on with it. The only other argument I
3920 Holidays (Waitangi & ANZAC Days) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
have heard put forward by the members oppos ite, outside this Chamber, is that it
somehow demeans the day. That is rubbis h. We know that they Mondayise Anzac Day
and their national day in Australia, and atte ndances at both even ts have gone up. In
2010 when Christmas was celebrated on a weekend no one thought the celebration
should be put off. They celebrated it on 25 December, and the celebration was no less
sincere because the day fell on a weekend a nd because they got an extra holiday and
some time with their families on the day after Boxing Day.
It is interesting that today Mind Your Own Business released the results of a survey
it conducted last year, when it asked its me mbers—businesses—what they thought of
the proposal to Mondayise, and 50 percent of small to medium-sized enterprise business
owners said they supported  the idea of Mondayising pub lic holidays that fall on a
weekend. Just 13 percent opposed the policy. So 87 percent of small-business owners
felt that it was either neut ral or a beneficial thing, a nd that is because good business
owners tend to take a positive view of policies that support their employees.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: That’s right; they do.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: That is right, and I am quoti ng from the press release here:
“the majority of business owners believe that the benefits to their employees—in having
time off to spend with friends and family—a nd the productivity gains that come from a
positive work life balance, are worth investing in.” The Labour Party agrees with that
view.
There are benefits, we have heard, as well,  for domestic tourism. As chief executive
Martin Snedden highlighted yesterday, $36 million accrues to the economy with each of
these holidays, and the Minister  of Tourism, John Key, has to stand up to that industry
and explain why he does not think they should get that benefit. It seems more and more
that the National Government is getting offs ide not only with workers, by stealing their
holidays from them, but also with employer groups.
The most important thing, though, that this legislation does is give hard-working
Kiwis a little more time with their familie s. Kiwis work amongst the longest hours in
the OECD. They work 1 or 2 hours extra every week more than their Australian
counterparts, and they get paid less. We  know that there is a correlation between
productivity and countries that value thei r workforces. There are benefits to the
economy of having well-educated, well-rested, and productive workers.
I want to thank the parties around the Parlia ment for their support for this bill: my
Labour colleagues, of course, the Greens, New Zealand First, the M āori Party, United
Future, and Mana. These par ties have heard the voice of  New Zealanders, unlike the
party of Grinches opposite us. My bill correct s an anomaly. It offers the full recognition
to Waitangi Day and Anzac Day that they de serve, and it ensures hard-working Kiwis
get the holidays they deserve every year.

25 Jul 2012 Joint Family Homes Repeal Bill 3921
First Reading
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I move, That the Joint Family Homes
Repeal Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice and Electoral Committee to
