items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: T ēnā koutou katoa. Ng ā
mihi nui o Te Wiki o Te Reo M āori. Let me begin, in speaking to this Parental Leave
and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Pa id Leave) Amendment Bill, by asserting
that the Government supports parents being ab le to look after their children. What is
more, we spent $157 million on providing the current 14 weeks’ paid parental leave in
the 2011-12 year.
I understand completely why community groups will express tomorrow—and have
already expressed—their support for paid parental leave, but , equally, at the same time
as they will say that they support it, those same groups have a sense of understanding of
the tight fiscal constraints that this Government is in at the moment. That is why we are
still seeing such strong s upport in the polls for the op tions that this National
Government is taking, not the continual stri ng of “Let’s spend on this, let’s spend on
that, let’s spend on something else.” Just because it is a good idea does not mean that
the money is magicked up out of fresh air to deliver it. We are concerned at the financial
implications of nearly doubli ng the amount of paid parent al leave, which has been
proposed in this bill.
This National Government is complete ly focused on responsibly managing the
Government’s finances. It is a pity that the previous La bour Government did not do the
same for the 9 years that it was in Governme nt. We want to get back to surplus. We
want to get debt under control. And what s eems anathema to the other side is that you
just cannot spend what you have not got, wit hout going into more debt and placing the
responsibility for getting rid of that debt on to  the generations to come. It is a choice we
have made, a choice we can live with, and a choice that we believe our grandchildren
will live with as well.
We have been dealing with the biggest de ficit New Zealand has ever had. It is too
soon for the determinations to be made about what new entitlements will be offered
when we get back to surplus. I am goi ng to focus on our priorities, which will
demonstrate that this Government has a str ong commitment to children and families, as
well. So that side should never accuse us of anything less. Go on, get on your hind legs.
My apologies, Mr Deputy Speaker—not you, of course.
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3947
We have worked hard during the last 3½ years, through a large recession, to preserve
income and support to families. We have—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am having extrem e difficulty hearing the
member. I would just ask members to contain themselves, somewhat.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: It is great to see the others on the other side are alive and
well. We have increased the maximum paid parental leave payment by $67 a week since
taking office. On 1 July this year the maximum parental leave payment available to
eligible employees and the self-employed increased from $458.22 to $475.16 a week.
The minimum parental leave payment for th e self-employed also increased. Employees
with at least 12 months’ continuous service with their employer are also entitled to up to
52 weeks of employment-protect ed, unpaid parental leave, le ss any paid parental leave
taken. This can be shared between eligible  spouses and partners. Up to 2 weeks of
unpaid partner’s paternity leave is also available.
I believe it is very important that I descri be this, because this is about what the
scheme currently offers. I would also like to reflect on some work that is currently being
undertaken—some conversations I have had with members of the Equal Employment
Opportunities Trust. They tell us that it is a ll very well to have paid parental leave, but
the important thing about paid parental leave is that it has to be managed in a way that
supports the reintegration of that  person back into the workfor ce. It is not just about the
money, actually. It is about feeling valued in the workforce. So when the employer goes
out of their way to make that person f eel supported, there is much more chance—
irrespective of how much paid  parental leave there is—tha t they will return to the
workforce. That is about flexibility and stagi ng re-entry to the workforce. That is about
encouragement, support, and, again, I say, flexib ility. That, in fact, will gain more than
just chucking more money at it, but then  chucking more money at it is certainly
something the other side of the House is  familiar with. And, boy, are their promises
mounting up.
We are continually improving the Working for Families scheme, which offers tax
credits to help families get ahead. We are committed to providing better health-care for
families, including free after-hours genera l practitioner visits for under-sixes, and
delivering record rates of i mmunisations for under-twos. Ag ain, what might that look
like? Children at the heart of policy is wh at that looks like. We have provided $54
million to boost maternity services to support new parents. What might that look like?
Children at the heart of policy—children and families. PlunketLine is fully funded 24
hours a day, 7 days a week to  support new parents. Did th at happen under the previous
Government? No, that happened under this National Government. Labour cut
PlunketLine. There has been a 34 percent in crease in early childhood education funding
since 2008. The Government spent $1.4 billion on early childhood education.
One of the things that I learnt when I was overseas last week is the unenviable, the
absolute—[Interruption] Last week, when I was away, I was made aware of what an
incredible record this c ountry has for the provision of  early childhood education—95
percent of New Zealand’s children have been engaged in early childhood education
prior to going to school. And, we, the Nationa l Government, have set a target of 98
percent. The UN committee could not believe  that a Government would show such
commitment to early childhood education. [ Interruption] The other side of the House
are hating that a lot; they certainly are. We have set aside an extra $19.1 million over 4
years to support Māori-medium early childhood education services.
The money that this Government has prioriti sed is prioritised into those who need it
the most. The best bang for buck in terms of  early childhood education spend is on the
children who do not currently get any—tha t is nil; no early childhood education. The
best bang for buck will be there. That is  why we have allocated $18.9 million for 1,039
3948 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
new places in high-need areas. New Zealand has a proud record in regard to early
childhood education.
I want to move on to the La bour Party’s costings. The ph ased policy in this bill
would cost $450 million extra over its first 4 years. Labour’s own costings: an extra $50
million in the first year, $100 million on top of that in the second year, and $150 million
more in each of the third and fourth years. We do not have that money. New Zealanders
know we do not have that money. The dangers of running up high deficits through
unaffordable government are simply not worth it.
The leader of the Labour Party, David Shearer, promised to run a thrifty Government
if elected. Actually, this is not a good way to get started, Mr Shearer. In 2007 the
Families Commission gave Ruth Dyson, then Minister of Labour, a report that
recommended paid parental leave provisions  be increased to 13 months by 2015,
including a month for fathers. Labour did not do anything with that. But now those
members sit on the other side  of the House and berate us. I believe that I have
demonstrated, and I know other members on this side will continue to demonstrate, that
children are at the centre of our policy, and we have put our money where our mouth is.
We cannot afford this policy at the moment , and therefore we are putting money into
other things that we believe will benefit children and the families of New Zealand.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: We come to the 5-minute calls.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I want to come back to a member of this House
who has a true focus on women, on children, an d on families—I want to pay tribute to
Sue Moroney. This would be one of the first occasions I have stood up in this House
and felt truly proud to speak to a bill and a po licy that I think will contribute to children
and to the betterment of their families, and I thank Sue for being the champion of the
bill, the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave)
Amendment Bill. I think she demonstrates her and Labour’s belief in, and focus on,
children. Our vision is that New Zealand not only be the best place in the world for
children to grow up but also the best place in the world to be a child, and that is key to
our vision.
What did we hear from that side of th e House, from the Mi nister of Women’s
Affairs? Her vision, during Sue Moroney’s speech, amounted to he r yelling across the
House “Will you mine?”. That was the interj ection we heard from the Minister of
Women’s Affairs: “Will you mine?”. The Minist er of Women’s Affairs is essentially
asking us the question, coal or children? Well, I ha ve an answer for that Minister, and
my answer is this: stop subsidising heavy polluters and we can back kids; build one less
road of national significance that we do not need and we  can help kids and their
families. This Government has proven that its priority is not children. It has proven it
time and time again. To hear the Minister of  Women’s Affairs stan d up and justify the
Government’s position that it will not invest in children was absolutely appalling. It was
shallow, to say the least.
According to the OECD, New Zealand spends roughly 50 percent of the OECD
average on kids. Primarily that is because of the money that goes unspent on the early
years. Changing our paid parent al leave would go a long way to addressing that deficit.
But it is not just about investing in paid pa rental leave because that is what families
have told us they want; it  is also about the evidence.  Sue spoke strongly to that
evidence, but I just want to reiterate it. The first 6 months are known to be the most
crucial period of a child’s development that we could possibly invest in.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: You don’t say!

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Tau Henare points out “You don’t say!”. Do something about
it is what I say to the Government. You have got the evidence. Listen to your own Chief
Science Advisor and do something about it. The WHO has told us that it is not only
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3949
about necessity, trying to encourage and a ssist women to breastf eed, but also about
attachment. We have seen more and more that attachment disorder is something that we,
as taxpayers, are picking up later on in serv ice provision. We have heard that conduct
disorder, in itself, costs up to a million dollars  across the course of a child’s life. Those
first 6 months are crucial.
This policy is about investing to save, so you would have thought we would hear
something about it in the policies of the Mi nister for Social De velopment on the Green
Paper for Vulnerable Children. Well, one thi ng that you do not hear the Minister talk
about is the fact that, in reality, all children are, by default, vulnera ble, particularly in
their very, very early stages, and that some universal policie s pay extraordinary
dividends. Paid parental leav e is in that boat and so is  early childhood education, and
the Minister of Women’s Affairs feels content to talk about the importance of that, even
though that Government cut early childhood education spending—blatantly. Now, it
refuses to budge on this. They tell me that that  is investment in child ren in their critical
years. Well, all of the evidence sits counter to that.
John Key himself has acknowledged that  we are no longer giving families the
choices about caring for their own children. We are in a race to the bottom in New
Zealand for our families. We have a chance to turn that round. In fact, the evidence that
has come out of the Growing Up in New Z ealand survey demonstrates that 87.4 percent
of women took paid parental leave when they  had their newborn. Af ter that, they then
started taking other mixtures of leave—unpa id leave, holiday leave, sick leave—
because it was so important to them that they be able to stay at home with their child in
those early months.
There is a better way. Sue Moroney and La bour have presented that to the House
today. The fact that that Government will not support it sh ows its vision for children,
and shows that Labour will put children at the heart of its policy.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Kaiwhakaw ā. Me mihi au ki
te Whare nei.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. My acknowledgments to this House.]
I am pleased to stand in opposition to the Parental Leave and Employment Protection
(Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. I want to go through it with some quite
clear reasons. I do want to be very clear from the outset of this debate that this is not a
debate about the merits of paid  parental leave. This is not  a debate about whether this
Government has children at the heart of its interests. This  is not a deba te about our
commitment to children—it is ab solutely not. I want to go th rough that in quite a lot of
detail.
It is kind of interesting that the member who has had this bill drawn from the ballot
has been a member of Parliament for 7 years now—3 of those in Government. So if this
bill was so important, if it was her one sole purpose for being, I am highly surprised that
it has become such a priority now, 7 years later, when Labour is in Opposition. But, you
know, I think that is part of existen ce on “Planet Labour”. Labour does the most
important things when it is in Opposition—or at least it can promise them, because it
does not have to pay for them. That is what happens on “Planet Labour”, because
money grows on trees.
National is focused on responsibly managi ng the Government’s finances. We have
children at the heart of our interests. One of  the things we are committed to not doing is
leaving our children and gra ndchildren with mount ains and mountains and generations
of debt, which is what that si de of the House is happy to do.  This side of the House has
more interest in making sure that we do have an economy that is managed responsibly.
Given that a previous speaker made so me comparisons with other countries, I
thought it was worth touching on where the other countries sit with this currently. There
3950 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
are countries that have longer paid parent al leave entitlements than New Zealand’s.
Portugal has 17 weeks, Italy has 5 months , Greece has 17 weeks, and Spain has 16
weeks. I think those countries would be familia r to more than a few of us in the House
and those listening, and the disastrous economies that they are running currently. It is an
example of some of the Governments’ spe nding that is not sustainable. There are
actually some countries that ar e currently looking at cuttin g their paid parental leave—
they are looking at cutting their paid parent al leave. This Government is protecting the
existing entitlements. Even Germany, which is one of the stronger economies in Europe,
has had to make savings in its  paid parental leave entitlements. So it is not something
that is unique for us.
We have been protecting the interests of parents in New Zeala nd. The Minister of
Women’s Affairs, the Hon Jo  Goodhew, spoke about the array of things that this
Government is doing in terms of investing in children. That side of the House might not
be interested in listening, but there is a significant am ount of work that we have done. I
do not think that it should be belittled that in these diffi cult economic times we should
be protecting entitlements. I want to give you an example. When paid parental leave
was introduced in 2002 the uptake exceeded predictions. Some would say that is a good
thing—absolutely. But the diffi culty is it is yet anot her example of a spending
programme that Labour introduced  with no reality in terms of  what the financial cost
would be. It increased 175 percent between 2003 and 2010. So there was a 175 percent
increase and only 14 percent more babies.
I am proud to be a working mother. I wa s staggered to hear Labour member Mr
Prasad, in a debate last w eek, basically imply that moth ers were not capable of doing
two things at once. In the debate on the social security bill that member suggested it was
too difficult for mothers to work and that it was hard on their children. Well, this side of
the House believes that women are capable of doing more. The Minister of Women’s
Affairs has given you our record, and so I am more than proud to say that we are
opposing this piece of legi slation. We are managing th e economy in a strong and
sensible way. We are protecting our child ren, supporting our families, and making our
communities stronger. Thank you.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou ki te Whare. The
Greens will be supporting this Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’
Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. Our policy is for 13 months’ paid parental leave, and this
bill to extend paid parental leave to 26 w eeks is a good start in progressing that. If we
are going to look at where we  are going, we should look at where we have been. The
provision of 1 year’s unpaid parental le ave was introduced in 1987, and it was a major
breakthrough for families. Although it was not pa id, it meant that, if they could afford
to, a parent could take a year  off to be with their child and be assured of having the
same job there when they came back. That is the crux of the matter: being able to afford
to take time off to have your children and have enough time to bond with them. The
State sector at that time tended to lead on good employment practic es, and it still does,
and I hope that it continues to do so. It had some provisions for paid leave during that
time.
It was not until 2002 that the Labour-Alliance Government, with the then Minister of
Women’s Affairs, the Hon Laila Harré, intr oduced the first provi sions for 12 weeks’
paid parental leave. By 2006 that had extended to 14 weeks of paid leave. Since 2002 an
estimated 190,000 people, mostly mothers, have accessed those 12 or 14 weeks of paid
leave. Looking at the trend over the last few y ears, more people every year are using it.
Its introduction has gone some way towards easing the financial shock that happens
when a newborn enters the family and the in come of the parents plummets. I remember
my own experience when my son was born in  1994. His father and I shared 12 months
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3951
of unpaid leave, and, as well as adjusting to the new circumstances of having a helpless
infant that we were responsib le for, we also had to ma nage halving our income. We
extended the mortgage to cover that time off.
Today we are hearing the same arguments against 20 weeks’ paid parental leave that
we heard back in the 1990s—that we cannot a fford it. That was the same argument that
we heard in the 1970s about equal pay. We got those meas ures introduced, and guess
what? The economy did not grind to a halt. The country did not go broke, and the sky
did not fall in. We have become so used to thinking in the short term that we no longer
think of the long-term benefits. These long-term benefits will outweigh the costs.
There is no doubt that 26 weeks’ leave is good for babies. The World Health
Organization recommends 6 months’ breastf eeding as a way of improving and ensuring
physical and emotional health for the child. Kids who have a parent at home in their
first year or so actually have better cogni tion and fewer behavioural problems as they
grow up. That child-paren t attachment is critic al to the child’s longer-term prospects.
That child-parent attachment leads to less abuse, and less neglect of children. That is the
cost that we all bear as a society. We mu st create healthy, strong families as soon as a
child is born.
Twenty-six weeks’ paid pare ntal leave eases a family’s immediate financial stress.
Research has also shown that generous pa id parental leave results in more women
returning to the same job they left, which pa ys off for employers, who have invested in
those workers. It also means working mother s are able to maintain their ability to
provide for their families.
We really are slipping behind international be st practice with our paid parental leave
provisions. Last year Australia introduced 18 weeks’ paid leave, giving working parents
the opportunity to choose between that or opt for a “baby bonus” of $5,000. As our
population ages, it is crucial that we are ab le to attract workers and a skilled labour
force. To compete, we need to be able to provide the same, if not better, provisions than
are enjoyed elsewhere. We must  get over our short-term thi nking. If we invest in paid
parental leave, we will get good returns. It is good for the economy, it is good for
babies, it is good for families, and it is good for our labour market. Tēnā koutou katoa.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora anō tātau katoa tēnei rangi. Ki a mātau o te Pāti Māori he rangi whakaharahara tēnei.
E tautoko ake ana i te āhuatanga o te pire ki t ōna mutunga mai. He aha t ā tātau, tā te
pakeke i tēnei ao? E ai ki t ā wētahi ko tā te pakeke he tiaki i te tamaiti, i te mokopuna.
Nō reira k āre m ātau i te whakah ē i t ērā āhuatanga katoa. Ki a m ātau, he taonga te
tamaiti, he taonga te mokopuna. N ō reira me aro tonu t ātau katoa, ki ngā painga ka puta
ki wā tātau tamariki, ahakoa kei hea r ātau. Ko te mea nui kia tiakina paitia r ātau e ng ā
whānau. Ana kua puta te kōrero i te pō nei mō te āhuatanga o te putanga o te tangata āta
titiro ki ng ā tūpāpaku m ō tēnei mea m ō te wh ānau me ōna raruraru katoa. Koinei te
tikanga o tā mātau aronganui, kia tiaki i wā tātau tamariki.
Me manaaki i te tamaiti, koinei te mea pai o tēnei o ngā pire, hāngai tonu ana ki tēnei
pire. Ar ā, kia whakarahi ake, kia roa ake te āhuatanga o te, me k ī te w ā whakat ā o te
mea tiaki i te p ēpi mai i te 14 o ng ā wiki ki te 26 o ng ā wiki. He mea pai t ērā. Me whai

kēkē, matua wh āea rānei, ngā pakeke, kia taea ai e r ātau te whiriwhiri te huarahi e tika
ana mō rātau. Kia kore r ātau e herea i ng ā momo pire. E hia k ē nei ngā kōrero kua puta
mō te āhuatanga o te nui o te moni. Kua raruraru katoa t ēnei pire n ā te āhuatanga o te
moni. Heoi anō, ko tā mātau titiro kē ki te painga o te tamaiti, o te mokopuna. Kaua ko
te moni i tōna kotahi.
Nā, pīrangi ana au ki te whakaara ake i tētahi kōrero, e hāngai tonu ana ki tētahi kupu
i Te Reo M āori. Ko te kupu, ko t ēnei kupu ko te “wh āngai”. He aha te wh āngai? Ko te
3952 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
whāngai, he mea tiakina e t ētahi o te whakapapa o taua tamaiti. He rerek ē ki t ērā o te
kupu “adoption” e ai ki t ā te kupu P ākehā. Ko te wh āngai an ō te wh āngai, ko te
adoption anō te adoption. He aha te rerek ētanga? Ko te whāngai, he tamaiti ka tiakina e
tōna whānau ā-whakapapa. Engari anō te adoption, ka taea e te tamaiti te noho nei, i te
taha o t ētahi ō waho ake o te whakapapa. N ō reira ko t āku ko te whakaara ake i t ēnei
take o te whāngai, i te mea ehara tērā āhuatanga i roto i te ture i tēnei wā.
Nā, hei tauira ake. Ō roto i a au, ō roto o te Waiariki, n ōnātatanei i tae mai t ētahi
wahine ki a au. Me k ī mō tēnei wā ko t ōna ingoa ko Hine. I a ia t ētahi pēpi whāngai. I
whiwhi a ia i te w ā i whānau mai tēnei pēpi. I mua o te w ā i whānau mai te pēpi, i tono
ia kia whiwhi ai ia i t ētahi p ūtea hei āwhina i a ia, engari, k āre t ērā i whakaaetia. Ka
haere ki te tono p īra, arā ki te pīra, engari ko te kupu whakamut unga i hoki mai ki a ia i
Te Tari Mahi, e k āo. Kāre i te whakaaetia. Anei tana k ōrero i te reo P ākehā: “Whāngai
are adoptions in accordance with M āori custom and are not le gally recognised until an
application for adoption is lodged in accordance with the Adoption Act 1955.” N ō reira
i raro i tērā āhuatanga kua raruraru katoa a Hine.
I roto i Te Ao Māori, ko tēnei mea ko te whāngai he mea nui. He mea ō nehe, me kī i
tōia mai ki te whai ao, ki te ao m ārama i t ēnei ao h ōu. Engari, ka taea i roto i te
āhuatanga o tēnei kaupapa o te whāngai, kia tiakina. He aha te tikanga o t ēnei kupu o te
“whāngai”? E ai ki t ā te P ākehā, “to feed and nourish”. Koinei te tikanga o t ērā kupu.
Arā anō ētahi atu kupu. Ko te āta whai ko te tamaiti wh āngai. Engari, ko tā mātau ko te
kī atu, ā, he aha te hē o te whakaae, kia pērā rawa te āhuatanga o Te Ao Māori, ki tērā o
Te Ao Pākehā. Kia whai tonu tēnei mea o te whāngai, ki tērā o te adoption. Mēnā e taea
ana e t ētahi tangata te whiwhi p ūtea mō te adoption, he aha te rerek ētanga o t ērā o Te
Ao Māori, me kī, o te whāngai? Ko tā mātau ko te kī atu, karekau he paku rerekētanga.
E ōrite ana te tiaki o te tamaiti. Ar ā anō te oranga o te tamaiti kei mua i te aroaro.
Engari, he rerek ē te ao me k ī, te tirohanga o Te Ao P ākehā me Te Ao Māori. Nō reira
kei te whakaara ake t ēnei kaupapa ki a koe otir ā ki a t ātau kia whai w āhi tēnei kupu ko
te “whāngai” ki roto i t ēnei pire. Kei te tautoko ake i te pire, t ēnā koutou kia ora t ātau
katoa.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Greetings once again, everyone, today. This is an important
day to the M āori Party. We endorse this bill until its completion. What is our role—the
role of parents in this world? According to some, it is up to parents to care for children
or grandchildren. Therefore we do not reject th at stance, at all. In  our view, children
and grandchildren are treasures. So we all need to focus on the benefits that emerge for
our children, no matter where they are. The main thing is that families take good care
of them. There was a comment made this evening about the coroner’s report pertaining
to a family’s plight. This is our focus: on caring for our children.
We must look after children. That is the positive focus of this bill, which will extend
paid parental leave from 14 to 26 weeks. That  is a good thing. Solo parents, couples,
grandparents, aunties, and uncles should be able to make their own choice about the
best avenue for them so they are not bound by  various laws. There has been a lot said
about the costs of the parental leave price ta g, which hinders this bill. However, our
focus is on the welfare of the child.
I want to raise an issue that relates to a M āori term. That is the issue of wh āngai.
What is a whāngai? A whāngai is a child who is cared for by one of their kin members.
It is quite different from adopti on. What is the difference? Wh āngai are cared for by
their kin, but adoption allows children to live with someone who is not related by blood.
Therefore I wish to raise the issue of whāngai because it is not recognised by law at this
time.
Allow me to provide an example. Recently a woman came to me in my electorate of
Waiariki. We will call this woman Hine. Hine had a wh āngai baby, which she has had
since its birth. Before the baby was born she applied for paid parental leave and the
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3953
application was denied. She then appeal ed and received a response from the
Department of Labour that denied her appe al. It stated this in English: “Wh āngai are
adoptions in accordance with M āori custom and are not legally recognised until an
application for adoption is lodged in acco rdance with the Adoption Act 1955.” Hine
was in a lot of trouble under that situation.
Within Māori society wh āngai is a very important concept. It is an ancient practice
that has been brought into the modern world. However, with this bill that concept can
be protected. The term “wh āngai” literally means “to feed and nourish”. What is
wrong with bringing the M āori practice of wh āngai in line with the P ākehā practice of
adoption? If one can receive financial assist ance for adoption, what is the difference
from the Māori practice of whāngai? We say there is no difference at all.
The welfare of the child must be paramount . But there are differences between the
Māori and P ākehā worlds. And so I raise this issue with you and I urge all of us to
allow the term “whāngai” to be included in this bill. I endorse the bill. Thank you.]

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I rise on behalf of New
Zealand First to speak in support of this bill, the Parental Leave and Employment
Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill, but for reasons that are
somewhat different from those that have been  expressed to this point in the House. I
want to pick up on a couple of things  that have been said—firstly, on wh āngai. Having
come from a family who have benefited from wh āngai, through my mother and my
nanny, I absolutely believe that this is part of  a conversation that needs to take place. I
believe that by bringing this bill to the House, Ms Moroney may actually have
accidentally provided a platform for that conve rsation to take place. That would be one
of the reasons why New Zealand First believes  that this bill needs to go to the select
committee. The country needs to have a conversation. We need to talk about what is not
in the current bill and how we  can improve it, and however th is bill comes out the other
side of this select committee process, that is exactly what the select committee process
is for.
We also, with all due respect to the National-led Government, do not happen to
believe your numbers. We would like to see them. We had to base this on the numbers
we have been given to date , such as our class size num bers, and we cannot get any
numbers around our bonus scheme. So we would like to go through the select
committee process so that New Zealand First can actually get some hard data from the
officials here about how much this may or may not cost the country.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Ask the reference library.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Nobody in this House disagrees—not the National Party, not
Maggie Barry, not Labour, not anybody else—that mothers and fathers are important to
children. None of us disagree on that. This is  not a conversation about whether that is
important or not, but this is a conversation that needs to take  place, and that is why we
believe that the bill should go to the select committee, and we will continue to support it
to that stage.
I do want to say one thing, though, to Ms Upston—

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: Mrs. I’m Mrs.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Mrs. I beg your pardon. Thank you. It always needs to be
clarified. I want to say that I was a proud, non-paid, and technically unemployed mother
for 15 years. I am proud to have been that, just as much as you are proud to be a
working mother. There should be no convers ation between the two of us about which
one of those is a better thing, because there is  no better thing; they are both worthy. Part
of the conversation that need s to take place is about—and I believe that it was Ms
Goodhew who said it—value in the workplace. I would like to see some of the extended
conversation take place at the select committee about value in the home.
3954 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
This is about priorities. This is not a bout other countries—wha t other countries do,
how many weeks they do it in, and how often they do it—this is about New Zealand and
the things we prioritise and the things we value. We all say that we value children. We
all say—and we all believe it—that we value those early years in that relationship with
their parents. All that New Zealand First is suggesting to the Government is that it was
arrogant, it was paternalistic,  and it was dictatorial to co me out before a conversation
took place, where the public of New Zealand could particip ate, and say that it would
veto this bill. We suggest that you change  your mind. We suggest that if Ms Goodhew
is right and the New Zealand public identifies the fiscal conditions that we are in, then
they will come, they will present to us, and they will say: “Yes, it’s important, but we
think it can wait.” If Ms Goodhew believes th at of the New Zealand public, give them a
chance to make that statement.
New Zealand First supports this bill to select committee, and we will continue to do
so.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: T ēnā koutou e te Whare. We are
absolutely in agreement with many of the th ings that have been said in this House
tonight about new parents. This is a Gove rnment that is extremely supportive of new
parents, and I honestly believe that the intent  of paid parental leave—that it makes life
easier for working mothers to take a longer leave period from their job, which is good
for both the parents and the baby—is an excell ent thing. In fact, th ere is considerable
research to say that it is greatly beneficial to most families. We are completely in favour
of that and entirely supportive of new parents.
Let us have a look at the facts, because the misguided and misinformed moronics in
other parts of the Chamber have not been paying attention to the facts. This Government
has put its money where its mouth is when  it comes to looking after children and
families. We spent $157 million providing the cu rrent 14 weeks of paid parental leave.
That is just in the last financial year. We  have increased the maximum paid parental
leave payment by $67 a week since we took office. On 1 July of this year, just over 3
weeks ago, we also increased the amount of  money that is available—the maximum
parental leave payment available for eligib le employees and for the self-employed as
well. These are big gains. Look at the figures: $458 has now gone up to $475 a week.
The minimum parental leave payment for th e self-employed has also increased. These
are excellent measures.
Let us take a look at some of the moronic things that have been mooted in this bill: to
extend paid parental leave from the current entitlement of 14 weeks to 26 weeks. But
wait! There is more—there is more. Sue Mo roney has actually admitted again that she
wants to extend it up to 52 weeks. What does that mean? Let us just dust down the
Labour abacus. Labour members do not have mu ch call to add things up, because their
maths is always wrong. They are always just thinking “Oh well, if we get it wrong we’ll
just borrow a bit more.” Let us have a look at  it, using their own costings for the policy.
It will cost about $450 million over the first 4 years. We do not have that money. We
just do not have it. The leader sa ys that that is thrifty. That is their idea of thrifty? I do
not think so. This is not a group of people who are going to be in Government any time
soon, because the New Zealand public are not  silly. Under Labour’s plan they would
phase in this money.
Let us take a look around the world, shall we? Let us have a look at what other
countries have done and what it has cost th em. France pays 16 weeks of paid parental
leave. It has just announced what? Spending cu ts of €65 billion to el iminate its deficit.
This is just what other countries pay when th ey have to borrow to give parental leave.
Spain has 16 weeks’ parental leave, a nd a debt of what? Of €820 billion. Its
unemployment rate is 24 percent. This is th e kind of future that Labour has got planned
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3955
for our children and our families. This is La bour’s wisdom. Let us have a look at the
infamous Greece: 17 weeks of paid parental leave. What does it cost it? A bankrupt
economy that has just had €240 billion of bail out money from other countries. It is
borrowing for unaffordable policies and it is not sustainable.
Ireland has 26 weeks’ paid parental leave. It is cutting €6 billion from its spending. It
has cut public servants’ pay—Labour would love that, would they not? They would use
their union block vote pr etty swiftly there. And it pays about 5 percent—it has put up
VAT to 23 percent. The most ge nerous of them all, the gold standard, is the United
Kingdom, with 39 weeks of paid parental leave. Remember, this is not even close to the
52 weeks that those people actually want to br ing in. They want to bring it in by stealth.
It is unaffordable. The deficit in the UK is  so high that the Government has just
announced the largest spending cuts since World War II. Well, thank you Labour and
the Greens for supporting these ridiculous po licies. We are doing the right thing. As
happens so often, Labour is out of step with the tim es. It is cocooned. It is unaware of
cataclysmic upheavals and seismic activities.
I believe that there is a very good debate to be had on the merits of extending paid
parental leave. I believe that we can do th at once the books are back  in surplus so we
will not be joining the international ex amples who have borrowed to fund the
extensions. This is an  ill-advised bill for these times that is poorly executed and put
through, and I am very, very glad indeed for the children of New Zealand that we are
not supporting this rubbish.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I am delighted to have the
opportunity to speak in support of this bill, th is very important bill, the Parental Leave
and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid  Leave) Amendment Bill. I congratulate
my colleague Sue Moroney, who I know has work ed really hard on this bill. She is
supported not only by the majority in this House but also by child advocacy groups,
community organisations, business, unions, and working families up and down New
Zealand. In fact, this bill is supported by everyone except National and ACT. But they
have never supported paid parental leave. Maggie Barry perhaps needs to go and study
her own party’s history. At every opportunity it has voted against paid parental leave,
and you do not have to go back very far in the Hansard to find out what the National
Party members were saying about it, including the current Minister of Women’s Affairs,
who made a disgraceful speech—a disgraceful speech. She actually said in the debate in
2006 around extending paid parental leave to  the self-employed that it was like a
benefit, that women would be better off with a tax cut, and that it was just extending
welfare all the time. I mean, it was disgracef ul stuff that we have heard from the
Minister of Women’s Affairs.
Then we have heard the National Party blaming women and children for the global
financial crisis. Can you believe it? Can you believe it? I have h eard everything now.
The truth is that this Government woul d far rather waste money on tax handouts to
people who do not really need them than invest in future generations by ensuring that
they have the best start in life.
This bill will ease pressure on working parents, and, boy, do they need it at the
moment. It will align us with entitlements in the OECD and help prioritise the early
years of our precious  children’s development. Extendi ng paid parental leave will
improve the health of mothers and children. It will help working mothers breastfeed
until their baby is 6 months of age, wh ich is the World Health Organization’s
recommendation. It also helps prevent premature return to the workforce on the basis of
financial stress. It enables women to stay  connected to the workforce but have a
reasonable amount of time off with their newborn babies.
3956 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
Paid parental leave is an issue about families and children, but it is also a work rights
issue. The need for paid parental leave ha s sharpened over the last  20 years as more
women have entered the workforce, and here  I want to acknowle dge all the women and
men throughout New Zealand who campaigned fo r at least 20 years for paid parental
leave. And the campaign goes on. Paid parental  leave gives a worker the right to take
time out to recover from birth, to establis h breastfeeding, and to bond with their baby.
We do that by paying an entitlement that mi nimises the economic impact that forces
parents to return to work before the time is right.
We now know from a number of evaluations that our current 14 weeks’ paid parental
leave is too short. Parents are returning to  work early because of economic pressures,
and the negative impact of that cannot be exaggerated. There are strong and proven and
employment reasons for having longer paid pa rental leave. The goal of paid parental
leave is to support both  the maternal health of the mother and the baby, but the current
length of paid parental leave in New Zealand does not do it adequately.
People tonight have said that most other OECD countries offer longer periods of paid
parental leave than New Zealand, and ma ny provide leave at a higher proportion,
including Australia, which has now moved to 18 weeks and it is paid at a higher rate
than New Zealand’s. But unfortunately since National became the Government in 2008,
it has done the bare minimum on paid parental leave. The amount has increased because
it had to under the Act. It is an automatic increase. Y ou are talking about $20 a week
over some period of time. It is provided for cost of living increases only, as it had to
under the Act.
After being a world leader when paid parental leave was introduced in 2002 and
extended in 2005, New Zealand is now lagging behind, and we know that New Zealand
was criticised internationally just last week at the United Nations Committee on the
Elimination of Discrimination Against Wo men because of our record not only on
progress for women but also on paid parental leave.
All Governments have to make choices about priorities every day they are in office.
We say this Government is making the wrong choices and priorities. It is wasting
money on foolish ventures, on consultants, and on a crazy asset sale scheme. Well,
Labour’s difference is that we choose families and children. I support this bill.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call on this Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Mont hs’ Paid Leave) Amen dment Bill tonight.
Everybody in this House will agree that spendi ng time with your family is important. I
am a mother of three—a working mother—and every single moment I spend with my—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: All mothers are working mothers.

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: Sorry, what was that—every mother is a working mother?
They absolutely are. But I absolutely believe that every moment that we spend with our
children is valuable, especially when you ca nnot always be in th e home with them. We
are lucky we live in a country that puts a va lue on children and supports their parents. I
believe that families are the cornerstone of our  society, and we need to strengthen them
as much as we possibly can.
But this bill, this Labour bill, puts a co st on the taxpayer of $150 million a year, and
with Labour’s own costings, that is $0.5 bill ion of taxpayers’ money over the next 4
years. Where is this money going to come fr om? Well, I can tell you exactly where it is
going to come from. It is going to come from overseas lenders. We are going to have to
go into the international market place, borrow money, and pay back interest, and this is
money we cannot afford to borrow. The La bour Party wants to drive New Zealand
further into debt. It wants the country to  borrow more, it wants the country to spend
more, and it is doing it thinking it is just going to be OK. Well,  actually we cannot.
Having the State running up debt  does not help families. Borrowing more does not help
25 Jul 2012 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 3957
families. What helps families is smart policies and sound economic leadership, and this
is what this Government is delivering fo r the people of New Zealand and New Zealand
families. We need to get back into surpluses. We need to get back into the black, and we
are going to pay for the policies the right way, with money in the bank.
Under this Government, we are going to spend the taxpayers’ money wisely and
support families with holistic family polic y approaches. So wh at are we doing for
family policy, you might ask—not that thos e members are asking—but what would you
do for family policy? This is what we are doing. We have got free doctor visits for most
under-6-year-olds. We have got higher Working for Families payments. We are
spending—listen to this, Sue Moroney—34 pe rcent more on early childhood education
than was ever spent under the Labour G overnment. We are fully funding PlunketLine
24/7, which that Labour Government cut. We are boosting maternity services by $50
million for new parents and vulnerable parents, so they can go and get more access to
the services that they need to support thei r families. We have got the lowest inflation
rate since 1999, and how does that help familie s, Labour would ask. Well, it is pretty
obvious. Lowering the cost of living for New Zealand families is absolutely
fundamental for them to survive in these tough times.
So what are we going to do in the future, you might ask, for families, instead of this
$150 million one-off policy? Well, what we are going to do is target 98 percent of our
under-fives to attend ea rly childhood education over the ne xt 5 years. What a fantastic
start for our families. We are going to improve maternity services to get the access
better for those families. What a great start for our families. And by 2017 we are going
to increase infant immunisations to 95 percen t for 8-month-olds. What a great initiative
for families. There is a right time and a wr ong time to implement policy, and this is not
the right time to extend parental leave.
I just want to raise one i ssue about parental leave that has not been talked about in
this debate, and that is about the signals and the trends that we are hearing about coming
from the sector—from midwives  and health professionals in  the sector—about what is
happening. The trend we are hearing about is that parents now believe—we are seeing a
trend—that they are taking only those 14 w eeks that the Government is paying for.
Previously, families used to save. They used to plan to take the leave that they would
like to take with their families. So when we have policies like this we have to be very
careful to ensure that we do not send the message that parental leave is for only those 14
weeks; it is absolutely not. Thank you for the opportunity to speak tonight.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: As I was saying before I was rudely interrupted by the
bell before, during my maiden speech in Parliament I said that I wanted to improve
work-life balance for New Zealand familie s. This bill, the Parental Leave and
Employment (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendm ent Bill, will do that. It will do it in a
way that helps New Zealand children get the be st start possible, it will do it in a way
that supports working families at that critically important time in their lives, and it will
do it in a way that truly does value parenting. I want to thank those parties that have
expressed their support for this bill in the House tonight. I think there has been some
very rational and well-researched debate coming through from the parties supporting the
bill. I was, though, alarmed and, I will say,  actually surprised at the sheer venom
coming from the benches opposite , as this side of the Ho use strives to do something
positive to support working families.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: To get us more in debt—more debt.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: The sheer anger—led by Dr Nick Smith, I would have to say, but
challenged very, very quickly by Maggie Ba rry—coming from that side of the House
was something I was not quite prepared for. I have got to say that to me it demonstrated
an anger and a resentment towards working families that I thought was quite ugly. I
3958 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Jul 2012
thought it was quite ugly, because that Government was on the wrong side when it came
to the class sizes issue. It did not understand families’ needs then and it does not
understand families’ needs now with paid pare ntal leave. There is a bit of a theme
coming through.
But look, I think there was actually a lawyer in Kait āia who said it best. A Kait āia
lawyer by the name of Bryce Quarrie was quot ed in his local news paper, saying he was
not entirely surprised by finance Minister B ill English’s threat to use his power of veto
over this bill. He said: “When you’re a fa rmer in Dipton, you probably think women
should be at home making tomato sandwic hes for the shearing gang, anyway.”, and I
think he has hit the nail on the head, because as much as those members might try to say
that they support paid parental leave, the truth is and the f act is that the National Party
has always voted against paid  parental leave, even when Labour, when in Government,
was running such strong surpluses. When we were in Governme nt the National Party
voted against it on every single occasion. This is  not to do with affordability; this is to
do with ideology. It is to do with the toma to sandwiches and the shearing gang, and that
is where the National Party still sits on this issue. Yet it says that it wants to provide—in
fact, it promised the voters at the last election—a brighter future. Well, I put that party
on notice. Selling our State asse ts is not a brighter future. Increasing class sizes is not a
brighter future. Investing in children in those early years by exte nding paid parental
leave to 6 months is a brighter future. That is what New Zealanders are going to start to
see through very, very soon. In fact, I think they have starting seeing through it already.
I think on the odd occasion the National Pa rty did let its mask slip. Maggie Barry
called this ridiculous policy, at the same time as I am sure her speaking notes, her
research unit notes, were telling her “Please don’t say you don’t like paid parental leave.
Just pretend you do, and say it is all about th e cost.” We have already exploded that
myth, because, as I said at the very outset, that Government spends money on people
earning over $150,000—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: You still haven’t told us how you’re paying for it. Where’s the
money coming from?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I am telling you now, Mr Smit h. I am telling you exactly how.
The tax cuts for those people earning over $150,000 that they did not need is money that
should be spent on supporting working families.  That is exactly the money. Mr Smith
has challenged me to say where the money would come from, and I have said where the
money would come from. But here is an ev en better idea. The paid parental leave
allowance is $475 gross a week. We pay in childcare subsidies up to $588 a week for
those same babies to be looked after by stra ngers. I say let us put that money into
having their parents being able to choose to stay at home with them, and let them have a
choice.
This debate is about families, and I want  to take the opportunity now to thank my
family for being here. Three generations of my family are here today to support me on
this bill. My parents, Mary and Daddy Moroney, are here, who brought me up and, I
think, did a pretty damn good job. Thank you very much for being here. I have my
husband, Shane, who has come to support me fo r the first reading of this bill, and I
guess who you might call the peop le who gave me the persona l initiative for this bill:
my sons, our boys, Quinn and Logan. It is gr eat to have you here. You are all my pride
and joy, and that is what it is all about. It is about a mother’s love for her children. I
recommend this bill to the House. Thank you.
